priorFinding.note: Independently reproduced and extended: the prior finding named only the missing key. The second, independent kill — /api/status carries the key as a dict, so float() raises and the except swallows it — means fixing the wiring alone would not revive the alert.

findings.whatWorks: The other three ops checks (_check_circuit_breakers, _check_contract_health, _check_data_freshness) receive real inputs from server.py:11755-11762 and can fire. The 4h cooldown and recovery-alert machinery are exercised by tests and are sound.
findings.rootCause: Two functions named similarly: _scrape_status_payload() (the alert's input, built from the scrape_status global) and get_status() (the HTTP handler, which decorates that payload with derived fields). The alert was written against the HTTP response shape and wired to the internal one, and the derived field is a dict rather than the scalar the checker expects.
findings.requiredRepair: In server.py:11748 pass {**_scrape_status_payload(), 'scrape_success_rate_24h': _scrape_success_rate_24h().get('rate')} (or have _check_scrape_rate accept the dict and read ['rate']). Add a test that feeds the actual production payload, not a hand-built float.

verification.reasoning:
The reproduction runs and produces exactly the stated output. The mechanism is confirmed at HEAD: server.py:11748 passes `_scrape_status_payload()`, which (server.py:1290-1304) returns `dict(scrape_status)` plus stall_threshold_sec / run_timeout_sec / status_summary and nothing else; `scrape_success_rate_24h` is written in exactly one place, server.py:4352, inside `get_status()`, and its value is the dict returned by `_scrape_success_rate_24h()` (server.py:1104-1124). src/api/ops_alerts.py:46-52 short-circuits on both shapes. The alert is dead. That much is upheld.

Rescoped on three counts.
(1) Novelty is misstated. priorFinding.note claims 'the prior finding named only the missing key' and presents the float(dict) TypeError as a 'second, independent kill' discovered here. PRIOR-A07-F03 already states verbatim: 'Even if the key were added, get_status stamps it as a dict and float(dict) raises TypeError, which the except clause swallows into another None' — and even carries the same `float({'total':10,...})` reproduction. This is a clean confirmation, not an extension.
(2) userImpact ('the operator is not told when more than half the scheduled scrapes fail... every alert channel stays quiet') is false. Four other live channels cover the same condition: server.py:2516 sends an email on EVERY scrape exception ('Scrape failed: {type}'); server.py:2369 emails on a blocked partial scrape; the ops sweep's own `_check_data_freshness` IS correctly wired (server.py:11749-11762, threshold 3x SCRAPE_INTERVAL_HOURS) and fires when sustained failure ages the board — the finding's own whatWorks concedes this; and .github/workflows/health-check.yml:78-90 reads /api/status's dict correctly and emits ::warning when rate < 0.5. What is dead is one redundant aggregate-rate alert, not the failure signal.
(3) blastRadius is inflated. playersAffected:1092 is unfounded — no player value is affected by a dead alert. routesAffected:2 counts /api/status, which is not defective: it publishes a well-formed dict that its actual consumer (health-check.yml) parses correctly. Only the ops leg of /api/signal-alerts/run is affected.
P1 implies operator-visible loss of coverage; with four surviving channels this is a redundancy gap, so P2.
verification.whatWouldSettleIt: Apply the stated repair (pass {**_scrape_status_payload(), 'scrape_success_rate_24h': _scrape_success_rate_24h().get('rate')} at server.py:11748) and assert the ops sweep returns a scrape_failure alert when scrape_history holds >50% failures inside 24h. The severity question is settled by whether an operator with ALERT_ENABLED gets any email at all during a sustained scrape outage — server.py:2516 says they do.

findings.title: A partial scrape that the promotion guard REFUSES to publish is recorded as a success — same event name, same history outcome, same last_success_at, and it increments scrape_count
findings.claimUnderTest: server.py:2362 comment — "R-3: Block partial scrape promotion — don't overwrite good data with degraded data". The implied contract is that a blocked run is visibly not a good run.
findings.observed: On the blocked branch server.py:2380 calls _mark_scrape_success(elapsed, player_count, site_count, total_sites) before returning the OLD data. _mark_scrape_success sets last_success_at and last_scrape to now, clears error to None, sets current_step='complete', increments scrape_count, emits the event scrape_succeeded, and appends outcome='success' to scrape_history. The only distinguishing artifact is a second run_event 'partial_scrape_blocked' at warning level emitted immediately afterward. Every aggregate built on scrape_history or last_success_at — _scrape_success_rate_24h(), /api/health's last_scrape, /api/metrics' scrape_total — counts the blocked run as a clean success. Compounded by W23-F003: the guard only trips on total data loss, so reaching this branch at all means the scrape returned literally zero sites, which is the single worst outcome and it is filed as a success.

reproduction.command: sed -n '2362,2389p' server.py && sed -n '1013,1050p' server.py
reproduction.expected: A _mark_scrape_failure / _record_scrape_history("partial_blocked", ...) on the guard's branch
reproduction.actual: _mark_scrape_success(...) then `return latest_data` — line 2380 followed by line 2388

numericProof.formula: success_rate_24h = successes/total over scrape_history; a blocked run contributes +1 to BOTH numerator and denominator

findings.userImpact: An operator looking at /admin or /api/health after a total scrape failure sees a fresh timestamp, no error, and a 100% success rate. They conclude the pipeline is healthy and do not investigate, while the site serves last-known-good data indefinitely.

blastRadius.note: Data is preserved by design on this branch (`return latest_data`), so no player value is wrong. Corruption is confined to the /api/status (scrape_success_rate_24h, last_success_at, scrape_count, last_n_scrapes), /api/health (last_scrape) and /api/metrics (scrape_total) payloads. No frontend page renders any of these fields; /admin reads only featureFlags, idMappingCoverage and nflDataProvider.

priorFinding.note: Reproduced by reading the live code path. Adds the specific downstream consumers that inherit the lie (scrape_history outcome, last_success_at, scrape_count, /api/metrics.scrape_total) and the interaction with W23-F003.

findings.whatWorks: The guard itself does the right thing with the DATA — it returns latest_data and does not overwrite the good snapshot on disk or in memory. send_alert() is also called on this branch, so an email does go out if SMTP is configured. The defect is purely in the status/history bookkeeping.
findings.rootCause: The blocked branch needs to clear the 'running' flag and stamp a finish time, and _mark_scrape_success is the only helper that does that — so it was reused for its side effects rather than its meaning.
findings.requiredRepair: Split the bookkeeping: a _mark_scrape_finished(outcome) that both success and blocked-partial call, with outcome='partial_blocked' recorded to scrape_history and last_success_at left untouched on the blocked path.
findings.dependencies: W23-F003 (same branch); W23-F001 (the success-rate metric this corrupts is itself unread)

verification.reasoning: The mechanism is confirmed, and I went further than the finding's sed-only reproduction: I ast-extracted server.py's actual helpers and executed the blocked branch's bookkeeping. Every claimed side effect is real — outcome 'success' in scrape_history, last_success_at and last_scrape stamped now, error cleared to None, current_step 'complete', scrape_count +1, the event named scrape_succeeded, _scrape_success_rate_24h() returning rate 1.0, and _metrics.scrape_total +1 with scrape_failures untouched. PRIOR-A07-F04 is genuinely confirmed. Three things do not survive. (1) blastRadius playersAffected 1092 is not defensible in the finding's own terms: the branch's whole point is that it returns latest_data and does NOT overwrite the good snapshot, which the finding itself says under whatWorks. No player value is wrong; zero players are affected. (2) userImpact names /admin showing 'a fresh timestamp, no error, and a 100% success rate'. /admin does not render any of those fields — frontend/app/admin/page.jsx reads only status.featureFlags, status.idMappingCoverage and status.nflDataProvider, and no file under frontend/app, frontend/components or frontend/lib references scrape_success_rate, last_success_at, scrape_count, last_n_scrapes or run_events. The corruption lives in the /api/status, /api/health and /api/metrics payloads only; an operator has to read raw JSON to be misled, and when they do, run_events carries partial_scrape_blocked at warning level alongside the log.warning and the send_alert email. pagesAffected is 0, not 1. (3) The severity amplifier in observed — 'compounded by W23-F003: the guard only trips on total data loss, so reaching this branch at all means the scrape returned literally zero sites' — is refuted at the source. Dynasty Scraper.py:4251 builds active_sites from the static SITES config, and :5412 appends a sites_meta entry for every one of them with playerCount 0 when that scraper produced nothing. total_sites is therefore the configured count, not the surviving count, and `site_count < total_sites / 2` trips on ordinary partial failure (e.g. 3 of 8), exactly as designed. site_count=0 is one case, not the only reachable one. So this is a real monitoring/bookkeeping defect on a live production branch (scheduled-refresh runs every 2h) with three surviving out-of-band signals, no page surface, and no wrong number served to any user — P2, not P1.
verification.whatWouldSettleIt: A test that drives run_scrape_now through the guard with a stubbed scraper returning 3-of-8 sites and asserts scrape_history[-1]['outcome'] != 'success' and last_success_at unchanged. No such test exists — grep for 'partial_scrape_blocked' across tests/, scripts/ and frontend/ returns nothing, which is why the branch has been able to file itself as a success unchallenged.

findings.title: The "fewer than half the sites returned" partial-scrape guard degenerates to "block only on total loss": `sites` carries 2 entries on the live snapshot and only lists sources that already produced values
findings.claimUnderTest: server.py:2362-2363 — "Block partial scrape promotion — don't overwrite good data with degraded data when fewer than half the sites returned results."
findings.observed: site_count counts entries of result['sites'] with playerCount>0; total_sites is len(result['sites']). On the live snapshot data/dynasty_data_2026-08-04.json, `sites` is a LIST of exactly 2 dicts — [{'key':'ktc',...,'playerCount':500},{'key':'idpTradeCalc',...,'playerCount':900}] — so the test is `site_count < 1.0`, i.e. it fires only when ZERO sites returned data. Worse, sites_meta is built by iterating `active_sites` (Dynasty Scraper.py:5413), the sources that actually ran, so a source that is skipped shrinks the denominator with the numerator: the two sources that DID fail this run (KTC_TradeDB, KTC_WaiverDB, both 'partial' per settings.sourceRunSummary) are absent from `sites` entirely. Meanwhile the served board blends 21 sources (/api/status.served_source_coverage), none of the other 19 of which the guard can see at all. The guard cannot distinguish 'KTC returned 500 rows and IDPTC returned 900' from 'KTC returned 1 row and IDPTC returned 1 row'.

reproduction.command: .venv/bin/python -c "import json; d=json.load(open('data/dynasty_data_2026-08-04.json')); s=d['sites']; sc=len([x for x in s if x.get('playerCount',0)>0]); print('type',type(s).__name__,'total_sites',len(s),'site_count',sc,'threshold',len(s)/2,'blocks?',sc<len(s)/2); print('served sources:',len(json.load(open('docs/master-site-audit/evidence/W23/api-status.json'))['served_source_coverage']))"
reproduction.expected: A guard whose denominator is the ~21 sources the board actually blends
reproduction.actual: type list total_sites 2 site_count 2 threshold 1.0 blocks? False — and served sources: 21

numericProof.formula: block iff site_count < total_sites/2  =>  site_count < 1.0  =>  block iff site_count == 0

findings.userImpact: A scrape in which 20 of 21 sources collapse promotes cleanly to production. Every value on /rankings, /trade and /draft is then a near-single-source blend presented with the same confidence chrome as a full 21-source consensus, and the single-source haircut is the only thing standing between the user and a one-vendor board.

blastRadius.note: Conditional. On a partial in-process scrape that loses one of the two enabled browser sources, up to 1,092 rows on 8 pages would promote on a halved anchor set — but no such event is present in the live snapshot, so today's realized impact is zero. The GitHub Actions refresh path is separately gated by scripts/validate_scrape_sanity.py.

priorFinding.note: Confirmed with one correction: `sites` is a LIST, not a dict as the prior finding says — the arithmetic and the conclusion are unaffected. Extended with the second, worse property the prior finding missed: sites_meta is derived from active_sites, so failed/skipped sources leave the denominator rather than zeroing the numerator, and 19 of the 21 blended sources are structurally invisible to the guard.

findings.whatWorks: The guard's intent and its data handling are correct — on a true total loss it does refuse to promote and does return the previous snapshot. `served_source_coverage` (server.py:4350) already computes the honest 21-source count and its own comment admits `source_health` "cannot detect a degraded board".
findings.rootCause: `sites` is legacy scraper metadata describing the browser-driven sources only; the modern pipeline gets 19 of its 21 sources from scripts/fetch_*.py CSVs that never enter sites_meta. The guard was written against the legacy structure and never re-pointed.
findings.requiredRepair: Gate on served_source_coverage (or on settings.sourceRunSummary.enabledSources vs completeSources) rather than on `sites`. Compare against the previous snapshot's per-source coverage so a source dropping from 400 rows to 3 also trips the guard.

verification.reasoning: The headline reproduces verbatim and the core arithmetic is right: server.py:2358-2363 computes total_sites = len(result['sites']) and blocks on site_count < total_sites/2; `sites` is a 2-element LIST on the live snapshot, so the predicate is site_count < 1.0 — it fires only on total loss. That code path IS live (run_scraper is driven by the in-process initial_scrape at server.py:2619 and the 2h schedule_loop at server.py:2622), so this is not dead code. Two of the finding's supporting claims do not survive, and one of them is the load-bearing one. (a) MECHANISM WRONG: the finding says sites_meta is built from 'active_sites, the sources that actually ran, so a source that is skipped shrinks the denominator with the numerator'. It does not. Dynasty Scraper.py:4251 defines active_sites = [s for s, on in SITES.items() if on] — the CONFIG-enabled list, fixed before any run outcome. An enabled site that fails still emits an entry with playerCount 0, shrinking the numerator only, which is exactly what the guard wants. KTC_TradeDB and KTC_WaiverDB are missing from `sites` because they are not keys in SITES (Dynasty Scraper.py:1698-1711) at all — they are KTC sub-fetches — not because they were skipped this run. (b) USER IMPACT OVERSTATED: 'A scrape in which 20 of 21 sources collapse promotes cleanly to production' is false for the production refresh path. scheduled-refresh.yml runs `python "Dynasty Scraper.py"` directly at line 190 — server.py's guard is not in that pipeline at all — and gates the success()-conditioned 'Commit updated data' step on scripts/validate_scrape_sanity.py (line 481), a per-source CSV gate over CSVs/site_raw/*.csv that ERRORs (exit 1) on a >50% row collapse, an all-zero value column, or a sub-minimum row count. The 19 CSV-fed sources therefore DO have a promotion gate; it simply is not this one. On the path where server.py's guard does apply, only ~6 sources are refreshed at all (2 SITES + 4 inline fetchers at server.py:2215/2250/2285/2322), so the realistic escape it permits is 'one of KTC / IDPTradeCalc dies and the board promotes on the survivor' — 1 < 1.0 is False, so even a 50% loss of the two anchor markets promotes silently. That is still a genuine defect worth fixing (KTC is the TE++ basis anchor and one of the two pick markets) and the finding's requiredRepair is the right one, but it is a weak safety net with a compensating control on the primary path, not the 20-of-21 catastrophe described. Downgrading from P1 to P2 accordingly, and the blast radius is conditional on a partial-scrape event that has not occurred: no user sees a wrong number today.
verification.whatWouldSettleIt: Simulate the in-process path with SITES = {KTC: True, IDPTradeCalc: True} and a KTC result of playerCount 0, and show server.py:2363 evaluating 1 < 1.0 as False and promoting. That is the honest one-source-of-two escape. Conversely, if the in-process scrape loop is disabled on the prod box (i.e. only scheduled-refresh.yml ever promotes), the guard is unreachable in production and this drops to Scaffolded only — checking dynasty.service / prod logs for 'Scheduled scrape triggered' would decide it.

findings.title: verify-sharp-production.yml runs on EVERY push to main and always fails at `git add data/ops/...` because .gitignore excludes data/ — so its "Enforce healthy population" verdict step has never once executed
findings.claimUnderTest: The workflow's final step, "Enforce healthy population", is supposed to raise SystemExit when the Sharp production smoke is not healthy — i.e. this is the gate that makes a broken Sharp deploy go red.
findings.observed: The preceding step runs `git add data/ops/sharp-production-smoke.json`. `.gitignore:45` is a bare `data/` and only `data/ros/` is re-included, so that path is ignored. git refuses an explicitly-named ignored pathspec with exit 1, and GitHub Actions' default shell is `bash -e {0}`, so the step dies on that line — the `git commit` after it never runs and the verdict step, which carries the default `if: success()`, is skipped. `git log --all -- data/ops/` returns nothing: the directory has never been committed in the repo's history, which is what a permanently-failing add looks like from the outside. The workflow's `on:` is `push: branches:[main]` with `paths-ignore: [data/**, exports/**]` plus `workflow_run` after Deploy Production, so this fires on essentially every code push. Its wait loop is `for attempt in range(1,81)` with `time.sleep(30)` on each miss = 2,400 s = 40 minutes of billed runner time per push, under a 50-minute job timeout, ending in a red X that says nothing about Sharp's actual health. The other three Sharp diagnostic workflows share the identical `git add` bug, but they lose only their artifact (their commit step is last and is `if: always()`), and none of them runs on an unfiltered push to main — force-sharp-production-now, trigger-sharp-now-via-merge and trigger-sharp-no-environment all filter `paths:` to their own workflow file.

reproduction.command: bash docs/master-site-audit/evidence/W23/gitignore-repro.sh; git check-ignore -v data/ops/sharp-production-smoke.json; git log --all --oneline -- data/ops/ | wc -l
reproduction.expected: REACHED: git commit printed, step exit 0, data/ops/ present in history
reproduction.actual: "The following paths are ignored by one of your .gitignore files: data" / STEP EXIT=1 / .gitignore:45:data/ / 0 commits ever touched data/ops/

numericProof.formula: worst-case wait = attempts × sleep = 80 × 30 s = 2400 s = 40 min; verdict steps executed = 0 because the preceding step exits 1 under bash -e

findings.userImpact: No direct user-facing number. The consequence is that the ONE automated check on whether the Sharp cohort actually populated in production has never run, so /market/sharp-tracker can serve an empty or cohort_building board indefinitely with CI showing a failure that everyone has learned to read as "the flaky sharp job again".

priorFinding.note: The git-add-a-gitignored-path mechanism is CONFIRMED for all four workflows (also matches PRIOR-A16-F06). Two parts of the prior claim are REFUTED by the trigger blocks: only verify-sharp-production.yml runs on every push to main (the other three filter `paths:` to their own file and effectively never fire), and only verify-sharp-production.yml loses a downstream verdict step — the other three put their commit last under `if: always()`, so they lose an artifact, not a gate. The 40-minute figure is confirmed but applies to that one workflow (the other three cap at 120/30/20 min).

findings.whatWorks: scheduled-refresh.yml and weekly-narratives.yml commit generated data correctly by using `git add -f` / explicit negation, so the repo already contains the working pattern. The smoke's polling logic and its healthy criteria (sleeper_started AND ffpc_started) are reasonable.
findings.rootCause: The four workflows were written to persist a diagnostic under data/ops/ without noticing that `data/` is gitignored wholesale, and none of them used the `-f` that the repo's other data-committing workflows use.
findings.requiredRepair: Either `git add -f data/ops/<file>` in all four, or (better for verify-sharp-production) drop the commit step entirely and move the verdict directly after the poll — a per-push smoke result does not need to be in git, and `actions/upload-artifact` already covers it. Also reconsider the every-push trigger: 40 minutes of runner per code push for a production-state probe belongs on a schedule.

findings.title: The Sharp production smoke reports `unmappedAssets` from `dataQuality`, a key /api/sharp/market has never emitted — it is hard-zero on every run
findings.claimUnderTest: The smoke payload's ffpcMarket.unmappedAssets is supposed to surface how many FFPC assets failed identity mapping, so an ingestion regression is visible in the recorded result.
findings.observed: The workflow reads `(market.get("dataQuality") or {}).get("unmappedAssets", 0)`. src/sharp/market.py:410-413 emits the value under `coverage.unmappedAssets`, and the live payload has no `dataQuality` key at any level. The `or {}` plus the `, 0` default means the miss is indistinguishable from a genuine zero, so the field reads as a clean bill of health forever.

reproduction.command: curl -s -b /tmp/audit-cookies-w23.txt http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/sharp/market | .venv/bin/python -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print('top-level keys:', list(d.keys())); print('has dataQuality:', 'dataQuality' in d); print('coverage keys:', list(d['coverage'].keys()))"
reproduction.expected: has dataQuality: True
reproduction.actual: top-level keys: ['status','generatedAt','methodologyVersion','query','assets','cohort','coverage','formula'] / has dataQuality: False / coverage keys: ['platforms','unmappedAssets']

numericProof.formula: reported = payload.get('dataQuality',{}).get('unmappedAssets',0); the key is absent so reported == 0 for all inputs

findings.userImpact: Nobody acts on this directly — but an FFPC identity-mapping collapse would leave the recorded smoke saying zero unmapped assets, so the one artifact an operator would consult after a Sharp regression actively misdirects them.

priorFinding.note: Confirmed at runtime against the live /api/sharp/market payload rather than by reading code; the emitting site (src/sharp/market.py:413, under `coverage`) is named so the fix is a one-word change.

findings.whatWorks: The sibling reads in the same block — coverage.platforms.ffpc.transactions/.movements, cohort.*, len(assets) — all hit real keys and would report real numbers.
findings.rootCause: The workflow was written against a payload shape that either predates or was never shipped by src/sharp/market.py, and `.get(..., 0)` hides the mismatch.
findings.requiredRepair: Change to `(market.get("coverage") or {}).get("unmappedAssets")` and drop the 0 default so an absent key records null, not a health claim.
findings.dependencies: W23-F004 (same workflow; the step this feeds never commits anyway)

findings.title: /api/metrics.data_age_seconds and /api/health.data_age_hours measure time since the process loaded the file, not since the data was scraped — they are numerically identical to uptime and reset to zero on every restart
findings.claimUnderTest: frontend/components/StaleDataBanner.jsx:10 — "``data_age_hours`` — hours since the last successful scrape", and server.py:4508 — "R-1: Data freshness check — flag stale if no refresh in SCRAPE_INTERVAL_HOURS * 3".
findings.observed: Both fields derive from latest_data_source['loadedAt'], which _set_latest_data_source (server.py:1307-1315) sets to _utc_now_iso() — the wall-clock moment this process read the file — regardless of when the data inside it was produced. On a disk-cache load at boot that is server start time, so data age and uptime are the same number. Measured live: uptime_seconds 7401 and data_age_seconds 7401, byte-identical, while the snapshot's own settings.sourceRunSummary.finishedAt is 2026-08-04T18:20:04Z, making the true age 14,117 s. The staleness threshold is SCRAPE_INTERVAL_HOURS*3 = 6 h, so data would have to be 6 h older than the last RESTART to trip — a server that restarts on any cadence under 6 h can never report stale data, however old it is. The same loadedAt feeds ops_alerts._check_data_freshness at server.py:11749-11754, so the operator email inherits the identical blind spot. The correct timestamps exist and are already served three feet away: /api/status.source_health.sources[*].ageHours reports the honest 3.83 h per source.

reproduction.command: curl -s -b /tmp/audit-cookies-w23.txt http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/metrics | .venv/bin/python -c "import json,sys,datetime; m=json.load(sys.stdin); scrape=datetime.datetime.fromisoformat('2026-08-04T18:20:04.195690+00:00'); true_age=(datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)-scrape).total_seconds(); print('data_age_seconds',m['data_age_seconds'],'uptime_seconds',m['uptime_seconds'],'equal?',m['data_age_seconds']==m['uptime_seconds']); print('true age from sourceRunSummary.finishedAt', round(true_age), 'under-report h', round((true_age-m['data_age_seconds'])/3600,2)); print('data_stale',m['data_stale'])"
reproduction.expected: data_age_seconds ≈ 14117 (3.92 h), independent of uptime
reproduction.actual: data_age_seconds 7401 uptime_seconds 7401 equal? True / true age 14117 / under-report 1.87 h / data_stale False

numericProof.formula: reported_age = now - loadedAt (= now - server_start on a cache load); true_age = now - sourceRunSummary.finishedAt; error = server_start - scrape_finished

findings.userImpact: A user on /rankings trades off values that are hours older than the page admits: StaleDataBanner reads data_age_hours and stays silent, so a board that has not refreshed since a scraper outage looks current the moment the service is restarted — and restarting is exactly what an operator does when a scrape hangs. The staleness warning is suppressed by the very action taken in response to staleness.

blastRadius.note: playersAffected 1092 is not meaningful — no player value is wrong, only the freshness warning is delayed. routes: /api/metrics, /api/health, and the ops_alerts leg of /api/signal-alerts/run. pages 41 is fair since StaleDataBanner renders in AppShellWrapper on every page, but the effect is an absent banner, not a wrong number.

priorFinding.note: Not in the prior index. PRIOR-A06-F11 concerns /settings' 'Live' badge measuring contract presence rather than freshness; this is the sibling defect one layer down, in the number that badge's honest counterpart is supposed to use.

findings.whatWorks: /api/status.source_health.sources[*].lastFetched/ageHours are computed from real per-source fetch stamps and were correct on the live payload (3.83 h, matching the snapshot). SourceHealthStrip already prefers those per-source ages. The fix has a correct source of truth to point at.
findings.rootCause: latest_data_source['loadedAt'] conflates 'when this process obtained the data' with 'when the data was made'. That is the right semantic for the disk_cache/scrape_run provenance field it was built for, and the wrong one for freshness, but it is the only timestamp the health path reaches for.
findings.requiredRepair: Derive age from the payload's own settings.sourceRunSummary.finishedAt (falling back to scrapeTimestamp / date) in both /api/health and /api/metrics and in the ops_alerts call site, and keep loadedAt as provenance only. Assert in a test that data_age != uptime for a cache-loaded snapshot.
findings.dependencies: W23-F001 (the ops alert that consumes the same wrong number is itself half-dead)

verification.reasoning: The mechanism reproduces and is real: server.py:1307-1315 stamps loadedAt = _utc_now_iso() on load, and both /api/metrics (:4671-4700) and /api/health (:4509-4520) derive age from it, as does the ops-alert call site (:11749-11762). Today the equality still holds byte-for-byte (571 == 571) and the demonstration is now sharper than the author's: the loaded snapshot's own sourceRunSummary.finishedAt makes the data 6.25h old, PAST the 6h stale threshold, while /api/health reports 0.2h and data_stale False — and /api/status.source_health independently reports 6.17h from the same process, so the honest number is three feet away exactly as claimed. StaleDataBanner is app-wide (AppShellWrapper.jsx:94) and reads data_age_hours with WARNING_HOURS=6, so the silence is real. Rescoped on two points the finding overstates. (1) 'They are numerically identical to uptime' is not a property of the metric, it is a property of the disk-cache-only state. server.py:2414 re-stamps loadedAt on every SUCCESSFUL scrape, so in normal production operation (2h cadence) loadedAt IS the scrape-completion time and the reported age is honest. The identity is permanent HERE only because the audit harness monkeypatches run_scraper to a no-op — that half of the evidence is harness-shaped. (2) 'A server that restarts on any cadence under 6h can never report stale data, however old it is' is wrong as stated: after one restart the age restarts from zero and still crosses 6h six hours later, so a single restart DELAYS the warning by the data's age at boot rather than suppressing it. Permanent suppression needs sub-6h restarts, which is not a normal cadence. What survives is a genuine monitoring blind spot — the staleness alarm is silenced by the very action an operator takes during a scrape outage, and the ops email inherits it — but nothing on any board shows a wrong VALUE, and the failure needs a compound precondition (scrape failing AND a restart). That is P2 on this audit's scale, not P1: P1 here implies a present-tense wrong number on a surface a user acts on, and this is a delayed warning. Not fixed at HEAD.
verification.whatWouldSettleIt: Restore the scraper on a scratch instance, let one scrape land, and re-read /api/metrics: if data_age_seconds diverges from uptime_seconds and tracks the scrape, the permanent-identity claim is confirmed as harness-only and the residual defect is exactly the restart-resets-the-clock window. A test asserting data_age != uptime after a cache load (the finding's own requiredRepair) would pin it.

findings.title: /tools/source-health claims "Scraper status for every ranking source in the pipeline" and renders 4 sources; the live board blends 21
findings.claimUnderTest: The page's own subtitle: "Scraper status for every ranking source in the pipeline."
findings.observed: SourceHealthStrip builds its row set from `runtime.enabled_sources` (status.source_health.source_runtime.enabled_sources) — the legacy browser-driven scraper's source list, today ['IDPTradeCalc','KTC','KTC_TradeDB','KTC_WaiverDB']. The live board blends 21 sources per /api/status.served_source_coverage, and /api/status.source_health.sources already carries per-source freshness for 22 of them. The 17 sources rendered nowhere on this page include every rank-signal contributor: dlfSf, dlfIdp, dlfRookieSf, dlfRookieIdp, idpShow, fantasyCalc, dynastyDaddySf, dynastyNerdsSfTep, yahooBoone, fantasyProsSf, fantasyProsIdp, fantasyProsFitzmaurice, flockFantasySf, flockFantasySfRookies, draftSharks, draftSharksIdp, otcffbSf, pfkDynasty, fantasyNavigatorSf. Verified in a real browser with the protocol's request-interception topology: the page header reads "Sources · 4 · 4h ago · 2 issues". The exact failure mode source_health_alerts.py was written for per CLAUDE.md — "IDP Show prod cookie expired and the source went silently stale for two weeks" — is invisible on the only page dedicated to source health.

reproduction.command: curl -s -b /tmp/audit-cookies-w23.txt http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/status | .venv/bin/python -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); en=d['source_health']['source_runtime']['enabled_sources']; print('rendered by SourceHealthStrip:', len(en), en); print('served by the board:', len(d['served_source_coverage'])); print('freshness stamps available:', len(d['source_health']['sources'])); print('invisible:', sorted(set(d['served_source_coverage']) - set(en)))"
reproduction.expected: rendered == served (21)
reproduction.actual: rendered 4 ['IDPTradeCalc','KTC','KTC_TradeDB','KTC_WaiverDB'] / served 21 / freshness stamps available 22 / 21 invisible — browser confirms header "Sources · 4"

numericProof.formula: coverage = rendered / blended

findings.userImpact: An operator (or a user who navigates to /tools/source-health after noticing odd values) reads "Sources · 4 · 2 issues", concludes the two flagged KTC sub-feeds are the whole story, and does not discover that e.g. idpShow has been stale for a fortnight — because that source has no row on the page at all.

blastRadius.note: playersAffected recounted to 0 — no board value is affected, this is a visibility gap. pagesAffected recounted to 1: `grep -rn SourceHealthStrip frontend/` returns one non-test call site (frontend/app/tools/source-health/page.jsx:26); the component docstring's claim of an inline terminal strip is stale. sourcesWithNoRow recounted to 19 (21 set-difference minus the idpTradeCalc/ktcSfTep alias collisions with the rendered IDPTradeCalc/KTC rows).

priorFinding.note: The prior finding notes /settings' 'Live' badge contradicts /tools/source-health for the same source. That contradiction is real but the deeper problem is on the /tools/source-health side: it only knows about 4 of 21 sources, so for 17 sources there is nothing to contradict. New in this shard: the 19-source list and the browser-verified 'Sources · 4' header.

findings.whatWorks: For the four sources it does render, the component is good: it prefers the per-source ageHours over the aggregate, surfaces source_failures[].details.message inline, and (per its own comment) deliberately renders an explicit failure state on the page variant rather than hiding. server.py:4350 already computes and serves the honest 21-source served_source_coverage — the correct input exists and is unused by this component.
findings.rootCause: enabled_sources describes the Playwright scraper's run plan, which stopped being the whole ingestion story when 19 sources moved to scripts/fetch_*.py CSVs. The component was pointed at the run plan rather than at the board.
findings.requiredRepair: Render the union of served_source_coverage keys and source_health.sources keys, using source_runtime only to annotate which of them the scraper drives. Retire enabled_sources as the row set.
findings.dependencies: W23-F008, W23-F003 (all three descend from the legacy 2-to-4-source view of ingestion)

verification.reasoning: The observation is exactly right and I could not kill it. frontend/app/tools/source-health/page.jsx:25 carries the subtitle verbatim ('Scraper status for every ranking source in the pipeline'); SourceHealthStrip.jsx:100 reads `runtime.enabled_sources` and line 108 builds `entries = enabled.map(...)`, so the row set IS the legacy scraper run plan. Browser-confirmed with the protocol topology: header 'Sources · 4 · 6h ago · 2 issues', expanded row count 4. Not a harness artifact — `enabledSources` is persisted production state inside the seeded snapshot (data/dynasty_data_2026-08-04.json → settings.sourceRunSummary.enabledSources = the same 4). server.py:4347-4349's own comment corroborates the root cause ('source_health above is derived from the 3-source legacy sites list and cannot detect a degraded board'), and server.py:1503-1507 says the freshness map was stamped so 'the source-health page can render per-source ages' — the component uses it only to annotate the 4 rows it already has. So the defect stands. What does NOT survive is the severity framing and the arithmetic around it. (a) Blast radius: playersAffected 1092 is not defensible — no player value, rank or number on any user surface is wrong; this is a monitoring-coverage gap. pagesAffected 2 is wrong: grep shows SourceHealthStrip has exactly ONE call site (frontend/app/tools/source-health/page.jsx:26). The component's own docstring claims a terminal strip variant, but that usage no longer exists — the author appears to have believed the docstring. (b) Internal inconsistency: observed says 'The 17 sources rendered nowhere' then lists 19 names, while reproduction.actual says 21 invisible. The honest number is 19: the raw set difference is 21, but `idpTradeCalc`/`ktcSfTep` collide by case/alias with the rendered `IDPTradeCalc`/`KTC` rows. (c) userImpact overstates: the exact incident class cited ('idpShow silently stale for two weeks') is covered by an independent path — src/api/source_health_alerts.py, a 24h-per-source mtime staleness detector wired into the daily sweep at server.py:11782 — which emails on staleness whether or not the page has a row. The page is blind; the operator is not left with no signal at all. Rescoped to P2: single operator-only diagnostic page, zero user-facing numbers wrong, working alert backstop. 'Implemented but defective' is fair; 'Partially implemented' would be more precise.
verification.whatWouldSettleIt: Change SourceHealthStrip.jsx:108 to build entries from union(served_source_coverage, source_health.sources) and use source_runtime only to annotate which rows the Playwright scraper drives; then a browser probe of /tools/source-health should read 'Sources · 22' and the expanded list should contain idpShow. A vitest asserting rendered row count == len(served_source_coverage ∪ sources) would pin it.

findings.title: /api/status.source_health reports total_sources 2, sources_with_data 2, missing_sources [] for a board built from 21 sources — a 19-source outage would still read as 2 of 2 with nothing missing
findings.claimUnderTest: The field names themselves: total_sources / sources_with_data / missing_sources on /api/status.source_health assert a complete accounting of the board's inputs.
findings.observed: source_health is derived from the legacy `sites` array (2 entries on the live snapshot) rather than from the board. The live payload reports total_sources 2, sources_with_data 2, source_counts {ktc:500, idpTradeCalc:900}, missing_sources []. The same response's served_source_coverage lists 21 sources with real per-source row counts, and source_health.sources carries 22 freshness stamps — so the honest numbers are present in the SAME payload, two keys away. server.py's own comment at 4347-4349 concedes the point: "``source_health`` above is derived from the 3-source legacy ``sites`` list and cannot detect a degraded board." (Note the comment says 3; the live value is 2.) missing_sources is empty by construction because the denominator is whatever ran, so it can never name a source that failed to run at all.

reproduction.command: curl -s -b /tmp/audit-cookies-w23.txt http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/status | .venv/bin/python -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); sh=d['source_health']; print('total_sources',sh['total_sources'],'with_data',sh['sources_with_data'],'missing',sh['missing_sources']); print('served_source_coverage n =',len(d['served_source_coverage']))"
reproduction.expected: total_sources 21, missing_sources naming any of the 21 that produced no rows
reproduction.actual: total_sources 2 with_data 2 missing [] / served_source_coverage n = 21

numericProof.formula: accounted = total_sources / len(served_source_coverage)

findings.userImpact: Indirect but systemic: this is the field any external monitor, dashboard or on-call check would naturally alert on, and it is green in every degradation short of the scraper itself failing to start.

priorFinding.note: Not in the prior index as its own entry; it is the shared root cause behind PRIOR-A07-F02 (confirmed here as W23-F003) and the /tools/source-health gap (W23-F007). Recorded separately because the fix is different: the guard needs a new denominator, the page needs a new row set, and this field needs to be either recomputed or deleted.

findings.whatWorks: served_source_coverage is correct, complete and already served on the same route. source_health.sources (per-source lastFetched/ageHours) is also correct. source_runtime's partial/complete/failed source lists accurately describe the scraper run they cover.
findings.rootCause: Same as W23-F003: `sites` is legacy browser-scraper metadata, and 19 of 21 sources now arrive as CSVs from scripts/fetch_*.py that never appear in it.
findings.requiredRepair: Recompute source_health from served_source_coverage (with the registry as the expected set so missing_sources can actually be non-empty), or delete the three misleading fields and leave served_source_coverage as the single answer. Fix the stale "3-source" comment either way.

findings.title: refit-hill-curves.yml opens a GitHub issue with no dedupe and no auto-close, alone among the six issue-opening workflows — a persistent condition mints one duplicate issue per week forever
findings.claimUnderTest: The workflow's own comment at lines 180-185: "These issues close when a human runs `scripts/model_registry.py promote` + `apply`" — implying a bounded, self-clearing alert.
findings.observed: The step is a bare `gh issue create --title "$TITLE" ... || gh issue create --title "$TITLE" ...` gated only on the refit driver's exit code. There is no `gh issue list --search` dedupe and `grep -c 'gh issue close' .github/workflows/refit-hill-curves.yml` returns 0. The workflow is weekly (cron '17 6 * * 2'), and the two titles are constant strings, so a challenger that keeps clearing the gate — or a regression that persists — produces one identical new issue every Tuesday and none of them ever closes automatically. Every one of the five sibling workflows that opens an issue does the idempotent thing: audit-rank-form-drift.yml, intel-refresh.yml, scheduled-refresh.yml, e2e.yml and audit-identity-matches.yml all search-then-comment and all carry a `gh issue close ... --reason completed` step on the green path. refit-hill-curves.yml is the only one with create-and-forget.

reproduction.command: for f in .github/workflows/*.yml; do c=$(grep -c 'gh issue create' "$f"); x=$(grep -c 'gh issue close' "$f"); s=$(grep -c 'issue list' "$f"); [ "$c" -gt 0 ] && echo "$(basename $f): create=$c close=$x dedupe_search=$s"; done
reproduction.expected: every workflow with create>0 also has close>0 and dedupe_search>0
reproduction.actual: refit-hill-curves.yml: create=2 close=0 dedupe_search=0 — the only outlier among six

numericProof.formula: duplicate issues per year for a persistent condition = cadence × (1 - has_dedupe) = 52 × 1

findings.userImpact: No user-facing number. The operational cost is alert-channel decay: the issue tracker fills with identical "Hill refit: challenger cleared the held-out gate" issues, they stop being read, and the one week the alarm means something is indistinguishable from the fifty that did not. Since ADR-008 makes promotion an explicitly human step, this is the alert that is supposed to prompt that human.

priorFinding.note: PRIOR-A13-F14 reports 'No registry entry recorded since 2026-07-29 despite drift far above the threshold' and PRIOR-A07-F14 reports the refit audit trail stalling with 6 of 13 runs failing. Both are symptoms consistent with an alert nobody acts on; this finding names a specific mechanical reason the alert would be ignored. The duplicate-issue behavior itself is new to this shard and is provable from the workflow file alone (I cannot see the live issue tracker from this container, so the count of actual duplicates is unverified).

findings.whatWorks: The gating logic is sound — exit code 1 (challenger cleared) and 3 (regression alarm) are distinguished with different titles and bodies, refit_report.txt is embedded, and the run URL is included. The `|| gh issue create` fallback correctly handles a missing `calibration` label. The deliberate decision not to auto-commit promoted constants (ADR-008) is correct and is respected here.
findings.rootCause: The idempotent open-or-comment + auto-close pattern was written for scheduled-refresh.yml and copied into four later workflows; refit-hill-curves.yml predates or missed the copy.
findings.requiredRepair: Port the sibling pattern: `gh issue list --search "in:title <TITLE>" --state open --json number` → comment if found, create if not; add an `if: success()` close step on the exit-code-0 path. audit-rank-form-drift.yml is the closest template and already matches on title rather than label specifically so it cannot reach across and close these.

findings.title: scheduled-refresh.yml commits the data and dispatches the production deploy at steps 8-9, then runs the DLF-freshness assertion and both watchdogs at steps 10-13 — every guard except one is post-deploy, and none can roll back
findings.claimUnderTest: scheduled-refresh.yml labels step 6 "Validate scrape sanity (pre-commit gate)" and describes the contract-coverage watchdog as catching "the silent registry / enrich / prime-timing regression that let ``otcffbSf`` be fetched + committed yet absent from the live board".
findings.observed: Enumerating the job's steps in order: 6 Validate scrape sanity (the only true pre-commit gate), 7 retention prune, 8 Commit updated data, 9 Trigger deploy (`gh workflow run deploy.yml --ref main`), 10 Assert DLF freshness (`if: always()`), 11 Report freshness, 12 Staleness watchdog (`if: always()`), 13 Contract coverage watchdog (`if: always()`), 14 Alert on workflow failure (`if: failure()`). So three of the four data-quality guards evaluate AFTER the data is on main and the production deploy has been dispatched. When any of them goes red the workflow opens/updates a `stale-sources` tracking issue and stops — there is no revert, no re-deploy of the prior commit, and no call to deploy/rollback.sh anywhere in the workflow. The named regression (otcffbSf fetched and committed yet absent from the board) is by construction detected only after that exact commit has shipped. Compounding: step 9's `if: ${{ !cancelled() }}` means it runs even when step 8 was skipped by an upstream failure, in which case it inspects the PREVIOUS commit's message and can dispatch a deploy on a run whose sanity gate failed.

reproduction.command: .venv/bin/python -c "import yaml; d=yaml.safe_load(open('.github/workflows/scheduled-refresh.yml')); [print(f'{i:2d} {str(s.get(\"name\"))[:56]:56s} if={s.get(\"if\")}') for i,s in enumerate(d['jobs']['refresh']['steps'])]" && grep -c 'rollback\|git revert' .github/workflows/scheduled-refresh.yml
reproduction.expected: the coverage and freshness watchdogs ordered before 'Commit updated data', or a rollback path after them
reproduction.actual: watchdogs are steps 12 and 13; commit is step 8 and deploy dispatch is step 9; grep for rollback/revert returns 0

numericProof.formula: pre-commit coverage = guards_before_commit / data_quality_guards

findings.userImpact: A user on /rankings can be served a board missing an entire source for up to one full refresh cycle (2 h) plus however long a human takes to react to the tracking issue — the watchdog proves the board is wrong and the board stays live regardless. Because the failure mode is a MISSING source rather than a broken page, nothing in the UI signals it (see W23-F007/F008: the source-health surfaces cannot see 17 of 21 sources either).

priorFinding.note: Not in the prior index. Distinct from PRIOR-A07-F11 (docs describing a dead automation topology) — this is about live step ordering in a workflow that runs every two hours.

findings.whatWorks: A great deal, and it should be said plainly: the watchdogs themselves are real and correctly wired. Both run under `if: always()` so a partial earlier failure still produces a red X; `set -Eeuo pipefail` with `tee` preserves watchdog_freshness.py's exit code through the pipe; the failure handler greps the teed log so the tracking issue names the actually-stale sources rather than a generic blurb; the issue is idempotent (search-then-comment) and auto-closes on a green run. validate_scrape_sanity.py IS a genuine pre-commit gate and does block the commit. This is a good detection system placed after the publish rather than before it.
findings.rootCause: The commit+deploy steps were the original workflow; the watchdogs were appended later as detection, and the ordering was never revisited to make them gates.
findings.requiredRepair: Move 'Contract coverage watchdog' and 'Assert DLF freshness' before 'Commit updated data' — the coverage watchdog builds the contract exactly as server._prime_latest_payload does and needs no committed state to run. Keep 'Staleness watchdog' where it is (it reports on stamps that step 5 writes) but add a revert-and-redeploy path when it fires, or gate step 9 on the watchdogs' success rather than on `!cancelled()`.
findings.dependencies: W23-F003 (production's own in-process scrape loop runs neither watchdog, so the only coverage check anywhere is this CI one)

findings.title: deploy/apply_hardening.sh is the sole installer for the 1-minute liveness watchdog, the 5-minute uptime probe and the 02:30 state backup, and no workflow, deploy script or timer ever invokes it
findings.claimUnderTest: deploy/systemd/README.md:37 — "deploy/apply_hardening.sh installs/refreshes all of the above" — presented as part of the deployment story.
findings.observed: deploy/deploy.sh and deploy/bootstrap-production.sh both invoke deploy/install-systemd-service.sh, which renders 12 of the 13 timer templates under deploy/systemd/ plus the riskit-backup pair. It does NOT touch dynasty-healthcheck.{service,timer}, riskit-state-backup.{service,timer} or riskit-uptime.{service,timer} — those three are installed only by apply_hardening.sh, whose sole documented invocation is a hand-typed `sudo bash deploy/apply_hardening.sh` (its own header, line 19). A repo-wide grep for `apply_hardening` outside docs and its own body returns zero callers. Consequences if the manual step was ever missed or the host was rebuilt: the 1-minute backend liveness watchdog does not restart a hung service, the 5-minute external uptime probe never runs, and the 02:30 state backup does not happen. The running instance corroborates the shape of this: /api/uptime returns {"enabled": false, "last_check": null}. (That specific value is container state and is not itself the finding — the finding is that nothing in automation guarantees these three units exist on a deployed host.)

reproduction.command: grep -rn 'apply_hardening' --include='*.sh' --include='*.yml' . | grep -v '\.venv\|node_modules\|apply_hardening.sh:' ; echo "callers above (empty = none)"; for u in dynasty-healthcheck riskit-state-backup riskit-uptime; do echo "$u in install-systemd-service.sh: $(grep -c $u deploy/install-systemd-service.sh)"; done
reproduction.expected: at least one automated caller, or these three installed by install-systemd-service.sh
reproduction.actual: no callers outside docs; dynasty-healthcheck 0, riskit-state-backup 0, riskit-uptime 0 in install-systemd-service.sh

numericProof.formula: automated coverage = installed_by_deploy / total_units

findings.userImpact: If the backend hangs, nothing restarts it and nothing pages anyone — the site is down until a human notices. If the host is rebuilt from the documented deploy path alone, user_kv and session_store have no nightly backup, so a disk loss takes every user's saved team, watchlist and alert rules with it.

priorFinding.note: Independently reproduced by cross-referencing all 19 timer units against the two installers. Adds the precise split: install-systemd-service.sh renders 12 of 13 deploy/systemd templates plus riskit-backup, and the three orphans live in deploy/systemd (healthcheck), deploy/monitoring and deploy/backup.

findings.whatWorks: apply_hardening.sh itself is well-built — idempotent, has a --dry-run, and enables the timers it installs. install-systemd-service.sh's coverage of the other 12 templates is thorough and guarded (it checks for both service and timer templates and for required secrets before installing). Both scripts do their job; nothing joins them.
findings.rootCause: Two installer scripts grew independently — one for app units on every deploy, one for host-hardening units as a one-off — and the hardening set was never folded into the recurring path.
findings.requiredRepair: Either call apply_hardening.sh from deploy.sh (it is already idempotent, so this is safe) or move the three unit pairs into install-systemd-service.sh's render loop. Add a post-deploy assertion in deploy/verify-deploy.sh that `systemctl is-enabled` returns enabled for all three.

findings.title: ops_alerts.py's docstring advertises six alert conditions; the module implements four — the signal-alert-cron-staleness and SQLite-integrity checks do not exist
findings.claimUnderTest: src/api/ops_alerts.py lines 6-11 list six conditions, including "Signal-alert cron hasn't run in > 36h (expected every 12h)" and "Session-store SQLite integrity check fails".
findings.observed: check_and_alert() calls exactly four checks: _check_scrape_rate, _check_circuit_breakers, _check_contract_health, _check_data_freshness. There is no function for cron staleness and none for SQLite integrity, and no other module supplies them to this path. The docstring's parenthetical is also wrong about cadence: deploy/systemd/dynasty-signal-alerts.timer.template is `OnCalendar=*-*-* 15:00:00 UTC`, i.e. once daily, not every 12 h — so a self-check written to the advertised spec would have been miscalibrated anyway. With W23-F001, the live check count is effectively three.

reproduction.command: grep -n 'def _check' src/api/ops_alerts.py; sed -n '221,233p' src/api/ops_alerts.py; grep OnCalendar deploy/systemd/dynasty-signal-alerts.timer.template
reproduction.expected: six _check_* functions invoked from check_and_alert
reproduction.actual: four _check_* functions defined and invoked; OnCalendar=*-*-* 15:00:00 UTC (daily, not 12-hourly)

numericProof.formula: implemented / documented

findings.userImpact: Nobody reads this docstring at runtime. The risk is a maintainer trusting it: the signal-alert cron can stop firing entirely — taking the custom-alert, BDVM-signal, ops-alert and source-staleness sweeps with it, since all four piggyback on that one endpoint — and nothing is watching the watcher.

priorFinding.note: Confirmed exactly, and extended: the docstring's '(expected every 12h)' also contradicts the shipped timer, which is daily at 15:00 UTC — so both the check and its stated threshold are wrong.

findings.whatWorks: The four implemented checks are correctly structured, the 4-hour cooldown keyed in user_kv under _system_ops_alerts works, and recovery alerts fire once on clear. check_and_alert never raises, as advertised.
findings.rootCause: The docstring was written as a plan for six checks; four were built.
findings.requiredRepair: Either implement the two missing checks (cron staleness is easy — compare now() against the last signal-alert sweep timestamp already stored in user_kv) or delete the two bullets. Fix the 12h → daily discrepancy in the same edit.

findings.title: The FFPC Sharp crawl ships as two byte-identical timer templates in two directories with two different installers and the same 05:20 UTC schedule
findings.claimUnderTest: Implicit: one crawl, one schedule, one unit.
findings.observed: `diff deploy/systemd/dynasty-ffpc-sharp.timer.template deploy/ffpc-systemd/chase-upside-ffpc-sharp.timer.template` returns no differences — both are OnCalendar=*-*-* 05:20:00 UTC with RandomizedDelaySec=900. They are installed under different unit names by different scripts (install-systemd-service.sh renders the dynasty-* pair; install-ffpc-sharp-service.sh renders the chase-upside-* pair, which install-systemd-service.sh never references). Both service templates invoke scripts/crawl_ffpc_sharp.py. On a host where both installers have been run, the FFPC crawl fires twice within the same 15-minute randomized window every day, doubling outbound requests to FFPC and racing two writers into the same platform ledger.

reproduction.command: diff deploy/systemd/dynasty-ffpc-sharp.timer.template deploy/ffpc-systemd/chase-upside-ffpc-sharp.timer.template && echo IDENTICAL; grep -l crawl_ffpc_sharp deploy/systemd/*.template deploy/ffpc-systemd/*.template; grep -c 'chase-upside-ffpc-sharp' deploy/install-systemd-service.sh
reproduction.expected: one timer template, one installer
reproduction.actual: IDENTICAL; both service templates invoke crawl_ffpc_sharp.py; install-systemd-service.sh references the chase-upside name 0 times (separate installer)

numericProof.formula: daily invocations = number of installed timers

findings.userImpact: None visible to a user unless the double crawl trips FFPC rate limiting or the concurrent ledger writes corrupt observation counts, either of which would surface as a thinner or wrong Sharp Tracker board.

priorFinding.note: Confirmed by byte-identical diff. Confidence is medium rather than high on the IMPACT half only: I cannot observe the production host, so whether both installers have actually been run there is unverifiable from this container. The duplication in the repo is certain.

findings.whatWorks: Each pair on its own is well-formed — explicit UTC, randomized delay, Persistent=true.
findings.rootCause: The FFPC crawl was prototyped with its own installer under a product-branded unit name and later folded into the standard dynasty-* naming, without deleting the prototype.
findings.requiredRepair: Delete deploy/ffpc-systemd/ and deploy/install-ffpc-sharp-service.sh, and add a `systemctl disable --now chase-upside-ffpc-sharp.timer` to the deploy path so an already-installed duplicate is cleaned up rather than silently left running.

findings.title: dynasty-custom-alerts.timer's systemd Description says "Hourly custom-alert sweep" while its OnCalendar fires every two hours

The body comment two lines below the Description correctly says "Fire every two hours", so the file contradicts itself. reproduction.expected: Description and OnCalendar agree
reproduction.actual: Description=Hourly custom-alert sweep ... / OnCalendar=*-*-* 0/2:13:00 UTC

priorFinding.note: Confirmed verbatim from the template. Noting additionally that the file's own inline comment already states the correct interval, so this is a stale Description rather than a disagreement about intent.

findings.title: 28 of 89 scripts/ entrypoints have no scheduler and no production caller, including five validators whose whole purpose is to be a guard that runs
findings.claimUnderTest: Implicit: scripts/ is the pipeline's helper layer, so a script there is part of the pipeline.
findings.observed: Scanning 1,358 non-vendored files for `scripts/<name>` and `scripts.<module>` invocation forms: 39 of 89 top-level scripts are reachable from a workflow, a systemd unit template, a deploy script, a Makefile/Jenkinsfile/.bat, another script, or src/. 28 have no such reference at all (3 more are referenced only by tests). Most are legitimately one-off research (backtest_*, measure_*), and calling those dead would be wrong. The ones that matter are the five VALIDATORS and board-guards: validate_sharp_roster_percentage.py, validate_va_v2.py, validate_scoring_fit.py, board_invariance_hash.py and golden_board.py. A validator that no scheduler runs and no gate calls is indistinguishable from a validator that does not exist — the specific pattern CLAUDE.md's rule 6 asks to be called out. Two scripts also reference siblings that are not in scripts/ at all (measure_engine_value_divergence.py is reached only from scripts/audit/finder_migration_snapshot.py; persist_nfl_actuals.py only from scripts/audit/measure_usage_signal_rate.py), so their reachability runs through the audit subtree rather than the pipeline.

reproduction.command: awk -F, 'NR>1 && $2=="none" && ($5=="NOTHING"||$5=="TESTS ONLY")' docs/master-site-audit/evidence/W23/schedule-map.csv | cut -d, -f1 | wc -l; grep -E '^scripts/(validate_|board_invariance|golden_board)' docs/master-site-audit/evidence/W23/schedule-map.csv | cut -d, -f1,2,5
reproduction.expected: validators either scheduled or invoked by a gate
reproduction.actual: 28 unreferenced; validate_sharp_roster_percentage.py / validate_va_v2.py / validate_scoring_fit.py / board_invariance_hash.py / golden_board.py all show scheduled_by=none, read_by=NOTHING

numericProof.formula: reachable fraction = 39/89

findings.userImpact: Indirect. The board-invariance hash and golden-board comparison are precisely the tools that would catch an unintended repricing between refits, and neither runs, so an unintended board shift reaches /rankings with no automated tripwire.

priorFinding.note: PRIOR-A13-F07 makes the same shape of claim about the tier-threshold fitter specifically ('no fitter that can run'). This finding generalizes it across scripts/ with a full census. Confidence is medium because the invocation scan is a static text search: a script invoked via a shell variable, a fully dynamic path, or an operator runbook outside the repo would be misclassified as dead. The five validators were each spot-checked by hand.

findings.whatWorks: The 39 reachable scripts are properly wired — the 14 fetch_* scripts to scheduled-refresh.yml, the four sharp crawlers to their timer templates, refresh_playerctx/refresh_reception_depth/refresh_bdvm_projections/snapshot_consensus_edge to systemd templates, and check_env.py to seven workflows. The full mapping is in schedule-map.csv.
findings.rootCause: scripts/ mixes three populations with no naming or directory separation: scheduled production jobs, human-invoked research, and validators that were written for a gate that was never wired.
findings.requiredRepair: Wire the five validators to something (board_invariance_hash + golden_board belong in scheduled-refresh.yml next to validate_scrape_sanity.py; validate_sharp_roster_percentage belongs after the sharp-rosters timer), or move them to scripts/audit/ alongside the other explicitly-manual tooling so the distinction is visible.

findings.title: There is no human review layer: nothing in the UI can approve, suppress, annotate, re-run, diff or roll back a single suspicious output — the pipeline publishes and the pages render whatever it produced
findings.claimUnderTest: frontend/app/admin/page.jsx lines 1-15 — "operator dashboard for flipping feature flags, running one-off admin actions ... the infrastructure of 'one place for all admin levers' is the point."
findings.observed: Full inventory of every operator lever that exists. /admin exposes exactly three actions (Flush NFL data cache, Migrate signal state, Force-logout all sessions) plus a guest-pass panel; ServerStatusPanel adds one more, POST /api/scrape. The docstring's headline claim — "flipping feature flags" — is false: the page renders featureFlags read-only and there is no write endpoint for a flag anywhere in server.py (flags are env vars read once per process; CLAUDE.md itself says "Rollback: RISKIT_FEATURE_BDVM_ENGINE=0 and restart ... there is no runtime toggle"). Against the four capabilities the brief asks about: APPROVE/SUPPRESS — absent; the only quarantine in the product is pipeline-computed (row.quarantined, rendered dimmed on /rankings) and there is no route or control to quarantine, unquarantine or exempt a row by hand. ANNOTATE — absent; no note, reason or provenance field is writable on any player, source or value. RE-RUN — present but all-or-nothing: POST /api/scrape re-runs the entire scrape; there is no per-source or per-player recompute. COMPARE VERSIONS — absent from the UI; scripts/board_diff.py and scripts/golden_board.py exist and are exactly the right tools, and per W23-F015 neither has a scheduler or a caller, let alone a page. ROLL BACK A MODEL — CLI only: scripts/model_registry.py promote/apply is referenced from server.py and the frontend zero times. ROLL BACK A DEPLOY — CLI only: deploy/rollback.sh, invoked by no workflow. The nearest thing to a human gate in the whole system is ADR-008's rule that Hill-curve constants move only by a human running two CLI commands — a genuine gate, but one that lives entirely outside the product. Everything a user reads on /rankings, /trade and /draft is whatever the last pipeline run produced, with no interposed approval and no way to intervene short of shell access to the host.

reproduction.command: grep -n 'runAction(' frontend/app/admin/page.jsx; grep -n '"/api/scrape"' frontend/components/admin/ServerStatusPanel.jsx; grep -n '"/api/admin' server.py; grep -rniE 'approve|suppress|annotat|rollback|override' frontend/app/admin/ | wc -l; grep -rn 'model_registry' server.py frontend/app frontend/components | wc -l
reproduction.expected: controls for approve/suppress/annotate/compare/rollback
reproduction.actual: 3 runAction calls + 1 scrape trigger; 6 /api/admin routes (flush, force-logout, guest-pass x3, signal-state migrate); 0 approve/suppress/annotate/rollback matches under frontend/app/admin/; 0 references to model_registry from server or UI

numericProof.formula: UI coverage = present_in_ui / capabilities; the one present (re-run) is whole-pipeline only, not per-output

findings.userImpact: When the pipeline emits a wrong value — and this shard alone documents three ways it can do so unnoticed (W23-F003 promotes a near-total-loss board, W23-F006 hides its age, W23-F010 ships it before the coverage watchdog runs) — a user sees that number on /rankings and trades on it. The operator's only options are re-run the entire scrape and hope, or SSH to the host. There is no way to suppress one bad row, annotate it as suspect, or revert the board to the previous snapshot.

priorFinding.note: PRIOR-A06-F08 says /admin renders to any signed-in user because its load-time gate is a public endpoint — an access-control finding about the page that exists. This is the orthogonal question the brief asks: what the page can DO. Confirmed independently that the mutating routes are separately gated (POST /api/admin/* returns 403 for the non-allowlisted e2e-test-user, per AUDIT_PROTOCOL's note), so the exposure is of the read-only view; the capability gap recorded here is unaffected either way.

findings.whatWorks: What exists is honest about itself. The three admin actions are real, confirmation-gated, and write a visible in-session action log with HTTP status and response body. The guest-pass panel supports issue and revoke. ServerStatusPanel's scrape trigger works. /tools/ros-data-health and /tools/trade-coverage are genuine read-only diagnostics. And the deliberate human-in-the-loop design for Hill-curve promotion (ADR-008) is a real gate that the refit workflow respects — it just isn't reachable from the product.
findings.rootCause: The system was built as an automated pipeline with observability bolted on; the operator surfaces answer "what happened" and were never extended to "and let me do something about this specific thing". There is no persistence layer for per-asset operator state (no overrides table, no annotations, no approval status), so no UI could be built without one.
findings.requiredRepair: Smallest useful increment, in order: (1) a per-row operator suppression stored in user_kv or a new table, honored by the materializer the same way row.quarantined already is — this alone gives a way to pull one bad value; (2) surface scripts/board_diff.py as a /tools/board-diff page comparing the live contract to the previous snapshot, which makes 'is this run suspicious' answerable before acting; (3) a documented one-command board rollback (re-prime from the previous data/dynasty_data_*.json) exposed on /admin. Approve/annotate can wait; suppress and diff are what the failure modes in this shard actually call for.

findings.title: The audit's own skip census undercounts skip sites 6x (27 declared, 166 actual) because it greps only `pytest.skip(` and misses 139 unittest-style skip sites
findings.claimUnderTest: evidence/test-results-summary.txt says '## Static census of skip/xfail markers (skips are runtime, so this is the declared set)' and lists 27 lines, framing that as the complete declared skip surface behind a 6,278-pass green run.
findings.observed: The census regex matches only `pytest.skip(` and `pytest.mark.skipif`. The suite is majority-unittest, and 139 further skip sites use `self.skipTest(...)` / `unittest.skipIf(...)`, which the census cannot see. Total is 166 sites in 43 files. The three largest are invisible to the census entirely: tests/api/test_launch_readiness.py (26 sites), tests/api/test_single_curve_live.py (17), tests/api/test_draft_capital.py (17). A skipped test and a passing test are byte-identical in `pytest -q` output, and no workflow asserts a minimum collected/passed count, so the declared figure is what a reader uses to size the risk.

reproduction.expected: 27, matching the census in evidence/test-results-summary.txt
reproduction.actual: TOTAL skip sites: 166 in 43 files; top files test_launch_readiness.py=26, test_single_curve_live.py=17, test_draft_capital.py=17, test_source_monitoring.py=15, test_picks_end_to_end.py=12

numericProof.formula: actual = pytest_style + unittest_style

findings.userImpact: A maintainer reading the green run sizes the false-confidence surface at 27 self-skipping assertions and moves on. The real figure is 166, concentrated in exactly the modules that assert against the live board (launch readiness, the single-curve invariants, the draft-capital workbook). tests/api/test_draft_capital.py is NOT livedata-marked, so its 17 skip sites sit in the BLOCKING tier: if openpyxl or CSVs/Draft Data.xlsx goes missing, the only check that a Sleeper-traded pick moves auction dollars in the right direction evaporates into a green PR.

priorFinding.note: Prior counted 157 in 30 files at commit 9c5d972; I measure 166 in 43 files at e96c06ef with a superset regex (adds unittest.skipIf/skipUnless). The new half is that the MASTER AUDIT'S OWN evidence file re-introduced the undercount at 27.

findings.whatWorks: Every skip carries a human-readable reason string; none are bare. tests/consensus_edge/test_panel.py's 10 shallow-clone skips are correctly gated on an explicit `panel.is_shallow()` and do NOT fire in CI (pr-validation.yml:65 and deploy.yml:43 both set fetch-depth: 0).
findings.rootCause: The census was produced by a grep for `pytest.skip(` against a test suite that is majority `unittest.TestCase`.
findings.requiredRepair: Replace the census regex with the union pattern above, and add a `--collect-only` floor assertion to pr-validation.yml so a drop in executed-test count fails the gate.

findings.title: tests/roster_intel/test_real_rosters.py — 22 tests written to catch 'a constant masquerading as a score' execute in NEITHER CI tier, because the file they need is gitignored
findings.claimUnderTest: The module docstring: '``_positional_coverage`` once returned exactly 100.00 for all 12 teams — a constant masquerading as a score. Synthetic fixtures would not have caught that, because it only collapsed on live data. Every headline metric is therefore asserted to VARY across the real league.' Line 29 adds: 'Marked ``livedata``: they read the live snapshots and are excluded from the blocking suite.'
findings.observed: The module is doubly excluded and runs zero times in CI. (1) `pytestmark = pytest.mark.livedata` (line 59) removes it from the blocking gate `pytest tests/ -x -m "not livedata"` — measured: 22 deselected, 0 collected. (2) The advisory tier `pytest tests/ -m livedata` DOES collect all 22, but the module fixture skips on `data/public_league/nfl_players_full.json` (line 63, gate at 86-87), which is gitignored by `.gitignore:45 data/` — only `data/ros/` is re-included — and is not tracked by git. Measured: 22 skipped. So the exact defect class this file exists for (a metric collapsing to a constant only on live data) has no automated detector at all, in either tier.

reproduction.command: cd /home/user/riskittogetthebrisket && echo '--- blocking tier ---' && .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/roster_intel/test_real_rosters.py -m 'not livedata' -q --co 2>&1 | tail -2 && echo '--- advisory tier ---' && .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/roster_intel/test_real_rosters.py -m livedata -q -rs --tb=no 2>&1 | tail -2 && echo '--- is the input tracked? ---' && git ls-files --error-unmatch data/public_league/nfl_players_full.json 2>&1 | tail -1
reproduction.expected: 22 tests execute in at least one tier
reproduction.actual: blocking tier: 'no tests collected (22 deselected)'; advisory tier: '22 skipped in 0.12s'; git: "did not match any file(s) known to git"

numericProof.formula: executions = blocking + advisory

findings.userImpact: /rosters and the terminal render positional coverage, fragility, clogger value, entry rate, lineup score, positional deficit and the competitive-window probabilities. If any of these collapses to a constant across all 12 teams — the exact failure the file records as having happened once already — every team shows the same number and a manager makes roster decisions off a metric that is no longer measuring anything. Sixteen named guards, including `test_fragility_varies_and_is_not_the_old_constant`, `test_trajectory_axis_is_live_not_pinned` and `test_eligibility_join_is_complete_on_the_real_league`, are all inert.

priorFinding.note: Prior counted skips in aggregate. It did not identify that this module is BOTH livedata-deselected and artifact-skipped, i.e. zero executions in either tier rather than 'advisory only'.

findings.whatWorks: The two other inputs the fixture needs — data/sleeper_last_good.json and data/ros/aggregate/latest.json — ARE tracked, so the gate that fires is precisely the untracked one. The skip message names the missing artifact honestly.
findings.rootCause: `data/` is gitignored wholesale with a narrow re-include for `data/ros/`; `data/public_league/nfl_players_full.json` (12,201 entries per the docstring) was never added to that re-include list, and nothing cross-checks livedata-marked modules against whether their inputs survive a clean checkout.
findings.requiredRepair: Either `git add -f data/public_league/nfl_players_full.json` and re-include it in .gitignore (it is a static Sleeper player dump, same class as the already-tracked exports/latest/), or make the fixture fail rather than skip when the module is run in the advisory tier. Adding a CI assertion that the livedata tier reports zero skips would catch the whole class.
findings.dependencies: Coupled to W24-F003 (the livedata tier is advisory) — fixing only the artifact still leaves these 22 non-blocking.

findings.title: 286 tests run only in a `continue-on-error` step, and at least 46 of them open zero files under exports/, CSVs/ or data/ — pure logic exempted from the blocking gate by a filename rule
findings.claimUnderTest: tests/conftest.py:78-86: 'A handful of tests assert against the LIVE scraped board ... Mark these modules ``livedata`` so CI runs them as a NON-blocking advisory tier while the pure-logic suite stays the hard gate.' tests/test_livedata_policy.py exists to check 'the exemption list, checked instead of trusted'.
findings.observed: The marker is applied by FILE BASENAME (`item.path.name`), not by whether the test touches live data, so it exempts whole modules including their purely synthetic halves. Measured with a `sys.addaudithook('open')` probe over each livedata module: tests/scripts/test_fetch_flock_fantasy_rookies.py (24 tests) and tests/adapters/test_dlf_scraper.py (9 tests) open ZERO paths under exports/, CSVs/ or data/. tests/api/test_dlf_source.py opens exactly one (data/snapshots/ranks_last.json), and 9 of its 13 tests live in the two classes (TestDlfCsvPreprocessor, TestDlfCsvEnrichment) that build temp CSVs — the second of which tests/test_livedata_policy.py's own docstring records as 'STILL OPEN, deliberately not fixed here'. tests/canonical/test_ktc_reconciliation.py opens one file but carries 13 tests. Total collected under `-m livedata`: 286 of 6,326. The policy test pins only two historical cases (test_pick_rookie_anchor_core.py and test_footballguys_source.py) and has no general check, so a new over-broad entry is undetectable.

reproduction.command: cd /home/user/riskittogetthebrisket && PYTHONPATH=docs/master-site-audit/evidence/W24 W24_IOPROBE_OUT=/tmp/w24-io.txt .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/scripts/test_fetch_flock_fantasy_rookies.py tests/adapters/test_dlf_scraper.py 'tests/api/test_dlf_source.py::TestDlfCsvEnrichment' 'tests/api/test_dlf_source.py::TestDlfCsvPreprocessor' -p ioprobe -q --tb=no 2>&1 | tail -3 && .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/ --co -q -m livedata 2>&1 | tail -1
reproduction.expected: livedata-marked tests read live data; otherwise they belong in the blocking tier
reproduction.actual: '[ioprobe] 0 distinct paths under exports/ CSVs/ data/' with '40 passed in 0.23s'; and '286/6326 tests collected (6040 deselected)'
