findings.userImpact: A PR that breaks the DLF CSV preprocessor, the DLF scraper's HTML parsing, or the Flock Fantasy rookie fetcher's row mapping merges green: those 46 tests report in a step marked `continue-on-error: true`. DLF is a voting source on the live board and Flock supplies the rookie ladder, so the regression lands in production values with the PR check showing a tick.

blastRadius.note: 516 = union of live-contract rows carrying a dlfSf, dlfIdp or flockFantasySf vote (277/139/378). 40 not 46 pure tests — 46 counted all 13 of test_dlf_source.py, which opens data/snapshots/ranks_last.json. Only 240 of the 286 livedata tests come from the basename rule.

priorFinding.note: Prior named tests/api/test_data_contract.py (33 tests) and tests/adapters/test_dlf_scraper.py (9). The data_contract half WAS fixed — conftest.py:103-118 records the removal on 2026-08-04 as 'audit finding Q-1'. test_dlf_scraper.py was never removed, and I add two more modules plus an audit-hook I/O proof rather than a source read.

findings.whatWorks: The blocking/advisory split itself is sound and well-motivated (a yahooBoone row-count dip should not block every PR), and tests/test_livedata_policy.py does correctly prevent the two specific regressions it names. tests/api/test_pick_rookie_anchor_core.py is a real, verified rescue: 9 tests with 10 numeric-literal assertions, in the blocking tier.
findings.rootCause: tests/conftest.py:143 keys the marker on `item.path.name`, a whole-file granularity the file itself defends as 'one central, reviewable policy instead of editing ~16 files'. Correctness is per-test, not per-file.
findings.requiredRepair: Move the three pure-logic modules/classes out of _LIVEDATA_MODULES (the same split already done for test_pick_rookie_anchor_core.py), and generalise tests/test_livedata_policy.py to run the I/O audit-hook probe over every exempted module and fail on any that opens nothing under exports/ CSVs/ data/. The probe is 40 lines: docs/master-site-audit/evidence/W24/ioprobe.py.
findings.dependencies: PRIOR-A08-F09 (basename collisions) is still latent and would become active the moment a colliding basename is added: 6 collisions exist today (test_calibration, test_endpoint, test_replacement, test_scoring, test_service x5, test_store), none currently matching a livedata entry.

verification.reasoning:
The reproduction runs and the mechanism is real. Three of the finding's numbers are not, and I recounted all of them myself.

CONFIRMED. tests/conftest.py:140 reads `item.path.name` and :143-144 adds the livedata marker by BASENAME, so the exemption is whole-file. .github/workflows/pr-validation.yml:164 is the hard gate (`-x -q -m "not livedata"`) and :166-180 is the advisory step carrying `continue-on-error: true`. 286/6326 collected under `-m livedata` reproduces exactly. My own per-module audit-hook probe (rerun independently) confirms tests/adapters/test_dlf_scraper.py and tests/scripts/test_fetch_flock_fantasy_rookies.py open ZERO paths under exports/ CSVs/ data/, while the other eleven modules open 1-48 — so the author's targeting is right, not scattershot. findings.title: tests/consensus_edge/test_scoring.py:301 asserts a cached object's field against itself and cannot detect an unstable paramSetId
findings.claimUnderTest: `test_param_set_id_is_stable` — the name asserts that the content-hashed parameter-set identifier is reproducible across calls, which is what makes a payload's `paramSetId` a meaningful version stamp.
findings.observed: `self.assertEqual(params_mod.load()['paramSetId'], params_mod.load()['paramSetId'])`. `params.load()` memoizes into a module-level `_CACHE` (params.py:25) and returns it verbatim on any subsequent call with `path=None, refresh=False` (params.py:61-62). Both sides of the assertion are therefore the same dict object's same key — the equality is `x == x` on one object. A paramSetId derived from `id()`, a timestamp, or unstable dict ordering would pass this test unchanged, because the hash is computed exactly once.

reproduction.actual: 'same object: True' — load() returns the cached dict, so the assertion compares one value to itself

If it stopped being content-derived, cached responses and stored verdicts would be compared under a stamp that no longer identifies anything, and the only test named for that property would stay green. Impact is bounded because the `consensus_edge` flag defaults off (ADR-023).

The POSITIVE ones are the weak half: `assert 'canonicalConsensusRank' in src` (test_rankings_our_rank.py:99) passes if the identifier appears in a comment or in a branch that never executes; `expect(page).toContain('platform: source')` passes on a string in dead JSX.

reproduction.command: cd /home/user/riskittogetthebrisket && .venv/bin/python docs/master-site-audit/evidence/W24/greptests_scan.py | head -3 && echo '--- frontend ---' && cd frontend && grep -rnE 'expect\((src|source|page|pageSource|clientSource|route|text|css)[A-Za-z]*\)\.(toContain|toMatch|not)' __tests__ | wc -l
reproduction.expected: behavioral assertions
reproduction.actual: {"total_tests": 5867, "grep_tests": 104} and 40 frontend source-text assertions

findings.userImpact: Low individually, and this class is small (1.8% python, 1.1% frontend). The risk is concentrated in the cross-file wiring tests (`test_the_consumer_reads_the_key_the_producer_writes`, `test_both_callers_go_through_the_shared_resolver`), where a grep test reads as proof that two modules agree while proving only that a string is present in both.

priorFinding.note: Prior measured the frontend as 92.6% non-numeric across 97 files. I measure the current 104-file suite and separate the specific 'grep test' subclass from legitimate render/shape assertions, which the prior's numeric-literal counter conflated.

findings.whatWorks: The NEGATIVE grep tests are well constructed and genuinely useful: tests/api/test_rankings_our_rank.py strips comments before asserting absence (so an explanatory mention of a removed identifier is not a false failure), and tests/api/test_frontend_migration.py:37-40 matches on `def {symbol}(` rather than a bare mention for exactly that reason. Frontend fixtures are NOT tautological: frontend/__tests__/fixtures/players.js is hand-authored, and the four parity fixtures (faab_bid_parity_cases.json, signal_parity_cases.json, name_key_cases.json, trade_grade_parity_cases.json) are shared cross-language oracles that neither side may hardcode against.
findings.rootCause: Wiring between a python producer and a JS consumer has no runtime seam in either test suite, so a source grep is the cheapest available check.
findings.requiredRepair: For the wiring cases, replace the grep with a round-trip: build the producer's payload in python, write it to a fixture, and have the vitest half read the key off that fixture — the pattern faab-bid-parity already uses successfully.

reproduction.command: curl -s -w ' HTTP %{http_code}' -b /tmp/audit-cookies.txt http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/consensus-edge/players
reproduction.expected: 200 (if the server.py comment were true)
reproduction.actual: HTTP 503 {"error":"feature_disabled","flag":"consensus_edge", ...}

findings.userImpact: None for the end user (the flag is correctly off). The damage is to maintenance: a developer reading server.py at the router mount — the natural place to look for 'is this feature live?' — concludes the board is shipping, and may debug a 503 as a bug or re-run a validation gate that already failed. It also makes the code comment disagree with the ADR it is meant to implement.

findings.title: CLAUDE.md's three payload-size figures are each ~3x low, and the test that supposedly pins them runs on a fixture 71x smaller than production
findings.claimUnderTest: CLAUDE.md:806-809 — full contract '~4 MB uncompressed'; delta '~1.25 MB uncompressed, and to ~100 KB over the wire'; 'Regression test ... pins the delta shape, byte-size bounds'.
findings.observed: Measured on the live stack: GET /api/data = 11,953,535 b (11.95 MB); POST /api/rankings/overrides?view=delta = 3,918,195 b (3.92 MB) and 372,690 b gzipped (373 KB). The named test asserts delta_bytes < 55_000 on a synthetic fixture and its own comment repeats 'delta is ~1.25MB vs ~4MB full', so it propagates the wrong figures and could never detect the drift. The RELATIVE claim survives: 3.92/11.79 = 33.2%, i.e. 66.8% smaller, versus the documented '~70% smaller'.

reproduction.command: curl -s -b /tmp/audit-cookies.txt -o /dev/null -w '%{size_download}\n' 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/data'; curl -s -b /tmp/audit-cookies.txt -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/rankings/overrides?view=delta' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"sourceOverrides":{}}' -o /dev/null -w '%{size_download}\n'
reproduction.expected: ~4,000,000 and ~1,250,000 per CLAUDE.md

numericProof.formula: measured / documented

findings.userImpact: A performance decision gets made against the wrong number. CLAUDE.md's own Performance Rules mandate 'eliminate oversized payloads'; an engineer budgeting against '~4 MB' will conclude the contract is already lean and look elsewhere, while the real cost is 11.95 MB uncompressed on every /rankings load. AUDIT_PROTOCOL's own perf evidence file records the same 3x gap independently.

priorFinding.note: The audit harness measured the full-contract number in evidence/perf/api-data-payload-sizes.txt; the delta figures and the test-assurance half are measured here for the first time.

findings.whatWorks: GZipMiddleware is real (server.py:2670) and does the heavy lifting — 11.95 MB → 1.18 MB on the wire. The delta mechanism genuinely works and genuinely saves ~67%.
findings.rootCause: Figures were written once against a smaller board and never re-measured; the only test that mentions bytes runs on a fixture three orders of magnitude smaller, so nothing in CI is coupled to the real number.
findings.requiredRepair: Update the three figures in CLAUDE.md, fix the stale comment in test_source_overrides.py:631, and add a size assertion that runs against a realistic contract (or a CI step that curls the live payload and fails a budget) so the number cannot drift silently again.

findings.title: CLAUDE.md attributes 239 client-numbered rows to the 800-rank limit; the board never reaches 800 and every one of those rows is unpriced
findings.claimUnderTest: CLAUDE.md:679-681 — 'In practice that is players past the backend's OVERALL_RANK_LIMIT (800) — rows the backend deliberately left unranked ... This is a display ordinal for otherwise-unnumbered rows, not a ranking engine.'
findings.observed: Measured on the live contract: 1,092 playersArray rows; 740 carry canonicalConsensusRank; the MAXIMUM stamped rank is 740, so no row is anywhere near 800. Of the 352 unranked rows, 113 are picks (correctly suppressed) and 239 are non-picks — and 239 of 239 carry rankDerivedValue = null. They are unranked because the board could not price them, not because they fell past a depth cutoff. buildRows has no value filter, so each of those 239 receives r.rank = computedConsensusRank (an array index) in the # column.

reproduction.command: curl -s -b /tmp/audit-cookies.txt http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/data -o /tmp/c.json && python3 -c "import json;pa=json.load(open('/tmp/c.json'))['playersArray'];r=[x for x in pa if isinstance(x.get('canonicalConsensusRank'),int)];u=[x for x in pa if x.get('canonicalConsensusRank') is None and x.get('assetClass')!='pick'];print('rows',len(pa),'ranked',len(r),'maxrank',max(y['canonicalConsensusRank'] for y in r),'unranked_nonpick',len(u),'of_those_null_value',sum(1 for y in u if y.get('rankDerivedValue') is None))"
reproduction.expected: maxrank 800 and unranked rows explained by the limit
reproduction.actual: rows 1092 ranked 740 maxrank 740 unranked_nonpick 239 of_those_null_value 239

numericProof.formula: max(canonicalConsensusRank) over playersArray

findings.userImpact: The doc turns a data-quality gap into a design decision. A reader concludes 'the board is a deliberate top-800 and everything below is intentionally unnumbered', when in fact 239 rows failed to price and are being handed array indices as ranks. That is the difference between 'we stop numbering past 800' and 'we could not value 22% of the pool' — and only the second one prompts anyone to investigate upstream, which is exactly what CLAUDE.md's own 'Fail-fast on missing stamps' paragraph instructs.

priorFinding.note: Independently measured before opening the prior index. PRIOR-A01-F01 measured 216 client-numbered rows on its payload and made the same 800-vs-740 point; I measure 239 unranked non-picks on the 2026-08-04 contract, all with null rankDerivedValue. Same mechanism, same defect, one day of drift in the count. The remediation of the # column belongs to the rankings workstream; the documentation half is filed here.

findings.whatWorks: The suppression logic itself is right: backend stamps always win, picks are never given a client ordinal, and an active valuation overlay suppresses the ordinal entirely (dynasty-data.js:1394-1401). The rule 'no frontend ranking engine' holds for VALUES without exception.
findings.rootCause: The 2026-07-29 correction that added this paragraph explained the mechanism accurately and guessed at the population it applies to, without measuring it.
findings.requiredRepair: Replace the '800' sentence with the measured cause: 'rows the backend could not price (rankDerivedValue null) — 239 of 1,092 on the 2026-08-04 contract'. Then decide separately whether such rows should be numbered at all.
findings.dependencies: Coordinate with the rankings/materializer workstream before changing buildRows.

findings.claimUnderTest: CLAUDE.md:188-190 — 'This resolves Defect D-2 (docs/python-coverage-audit.md), which was open between "503 per this table" and "keep the fallback and fix the doc". Fixing the doc is the answer, and this is it.'

reproduction.expected: one consistent status verb; a profile guard in the handler

The cost is that the next person to touch multi-league draft capital reads whichever file they open first and either reopens a closed question or ships against a closed one that the code still treats as open. priorFinding.note: Reproduced verbatim at HEAD, including the sub-claim about the missing scoring_profile guard: the handler range has zero references while /api/data has one.

findings.title: meta.sleeperLoadedLeagueKey names the wrong league on a valid cross-league payload, and the documented 503/sleeper-null contract for terminal no longer holds
findings.claimUnderTest: CLAUDE.md:165-166 'meta.sleeperLoadedLeagueKey — which league the sleeper block *would* be for, when sleeperDataReady: false (diagnostic only)'; :169-172 'serve shared rankings with sleeper: null + sleeperDataReady: false'; :173-176 '/api/terminal, /api/trade/*, /api/angle/* — 503 whenever the loaded contract's leagueKey doesn't match'.
findings.observed: GET /api/data?view=compact&leagueKey=dynasty_new returns sleeperDataReady: TRUE, sleeper NOT null, and sleeper.leagueId 1320092771247222784 / leagueName 'Blood, Sweat, and Beers' / 10 teams — i.e. genuinely the requested league, fetched by the cross-league overlay path at server.py:3240-3263. And yet meta.sleeperLoadedLeagueKey is stamped 'dynasty_main'. The field is set inside the ready=True branch, guarded by `if not sleeper_matches`, so its meaning silently changed from 'which league the sleeper block is' to 'which league the base contract was built for' — the doc still describes the first. GET /api/terminal?leagueKey=dynasty_new returns HTTP 200 with dynasty_new's own teams, not the documented 503; POST /api/trade/finder and /api/angle/find with the same key do 503, so the rule now holds for two of the three families it names.

reproduction.command: curl -s -b /tmp/audit-cookies.txt 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/data?view=compact&leagueKey=dynasty_new' | python3 -c "import sys,json;d=json.load(sys.stdin);print(d['meta']);print(d['sleeper']['leagueId'], d['sleeper']['leagueName'], len(d['sleeper']['teams']))"; curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'terminal=%{http_code}\n' -b /tmp/audit-cookies.txt 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/terminal?leagueKey=dynasty_new'
reproduction.expected: sleeperDataReady false + sleeper null, or sleeperLoadedLeagueKey absent; terminal 503
reproduction.actual: sleeperDataReady true, sleeper present and correct for dynasty_new, sleeperLoadedLeagueKey 'dynasty_main'; terminal 200

numericProof.formula: sleeperLoadedLeagueKey should identify the league whose rosters are in the sleeper block

findings.userImpact: No wrong number reaches a user — the rosters served are the right ones, and the cross-league overlay is genuinely better than the doc describes. The risk is inverted: a diagnostic field that names the wrong league will send whoever debugs a multi-league incident to the wrong league's data, and a developer trusting the 503 table may 'restore' a 503 on /api/terminal and delete working cross-league support to satisfy a doc.

priorFinding.note: The prior registry covers league isolation broadly; the sleeperLoadedLeagueKey mis-stamp on the ready=True overlay branch is measured here.

findings.whatWorks: The cross-league overlay itself is correct and well-built: two different leagues get two different sleeper blocks with the right ids, names and team counts, from one shared scoring-profile contract — exactly what the scoring-profile/leagueKey split promises. The degraded sleeper:null path still exists as the fallback when the overlay fetch fails (server.py:3287-3300).
findings.rootCause: A capability was added (live cross-league roster overlay) that made an existing diagnostic field's name inaccurate, and CLAUDE.md's error table was written for the pre-overlay behaviour.
findings.requiredRepair: Rename the field to what it now means (e.g. contractLeagueKey) or stop stamping it on the ready=True branch; rewrite CLAUDE.md's error table to describe the overlay path as primary and the null path as the fallback, and split /api/terminal out of the trade/angle 503 rule.

findings.title: ADR-001..015 exist in two DECISIONS.md files with unrelated subjects, and 36 of 44 ADR citations in src/ do not say which file
findings.claimUnderTest: CLAUDE.md:400-403 — 'NOTE: the ADR numbers are per-file, not global — there is a DIFFERENT ADR-008 in docs/league-intelligence/DECISIONS.md about replacement levels. Always cite ADRs with their file'.
findings.observed: The rule is correct and the codebase it governs breaks it. ADR-001 through ADR-015 exist in BOTH docs/league-intelligence/DECISIONS.md and docs/consensus-edge/DECISIONS.md with unrelated subjects — ADR-008 is 'replacement levels use endogenous flex allocation' in one and 'the mispricing component earned its place' in the other; ADR-015 is 'the TE alignment is now a measured basis conversion' versus 'market movement is the right target'. A third file, docs/roster-trade-intelligence/DECISIONS.md, contains exactly one ADR, numbered 008, with no 001-007. Across src/ and server.py there are 44 ADR citations; 36 of them use an id in the ambiguous 001-015 range with no file named, spread over 24 modules including src/bdvm/roster.py ('ADR-004/007'), src/api/gameplan.py ('ADR-011') and src/ros/lineup.py ('ADR-004', 'ADR-007').

reproduction.command: for f in docs/league-intelligence/DECISIONS.md docs/consensus-edge/DECISIONS.md docs/roster-trade-intelligence/DECISIONS.md; do echo "-- $f"; grep -oE '^## ADR-[0-9]+' $f | tr '\n' ' '; echo; done; grep -rnoE 'ADR-0[0-9]{2}' --include=*.py src/ server.py | grep -v __pycache__ | tee /tmp/adr.txt | wc -l; grep -cE 'ADR-0(0[1-9]|1[0-5])$' /tmp/adr.txt
reproduction.expected: one ADR namespace, or every citation file-qualified
reproduction.actual: ADR-001..015 duplicated across two files; 44 citations, 36 ambiguous, 24 modules

numericProof.formula: count of ADR-0NN citations in src/+server.py where NN in 001..015 and no file named

findings.userImpact: No user-facing number moves. The cost lands on anyone trying to change a tuned constant: CLAUDE.md tells you to read the ADR before touching the refit gate, and 36 of the pointers in the code lead to two different documents. In this repo that matters more than usual, because ADRs are where measured decisions (ADR-023 reverting a shipped flag, ADR-015 replacing a flat 1.15 with a measured curve) are recorded — reading the wrong one produces a confidently wrong change.

priorFinding.note: The ambiguity is noted by CLAUDE.md itself; the 36/44 measurement across 24 modules is taken here.

findings.whatWorks: The ADRs are genuinely good — dated, statused, with measurements and explicit supersession (ADR-015 'Supersedes the "no code change yet" half of ADR-009 for Axis A'). The problem is only the namespace.
findings.rootCause: Three subsystems each started their own DECISIONS.md at ADR-001 without a prefix.
findings.requiredRepair: Prefix the ids by subsystem (LI-ADR-008, CE-ADR-008, RTI-ADR-008), keeping the old numbers as aliases in each file's header, then sweep the 36 code citations. Cheap, mechanical, and it makes CLAUDE.md's own rule enforceable by grep.

findings.title: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md tells you to fetch /api/data?view=delta; that route silently ignores the parameter and returns the full 11.95 MB contract
findings.claimUnderTest: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:101-105 — 'Next.js renders shell ─► /api/data?view=delta ─► build_rankings_delta_payload(...)'.
findings.observed: GET /api/data?view=delta returns 11,953,535 bytes — byte-identical to GET /api/data with no view parameter — with payloadView null. It does not call build_rankings_delta_payload. The delta view lives on POST /api/rankings/overrides?view=delta, which CLAUDE.md:807 documents correctly. Two problems compound: the doc is wrong, AND the route accepts an unrecognised view value silently instead of rejecting it, so the mistake produces no error anywhere — just 3x the bytes.

reproduction.expected: delta materially smaller than none

numericProof.formula: bytes(?view=delta) - bytes(no view)

findings.userImpact: A developer following the architecture doc ships a request they believe is a compact delta and actually transfers 11.95 MB — double even the ?view=app path they would otherwise have used. The silent-accept behaviour means it survives review, CI and production without a single error line. This is the mechanism by which a documentation defect becomes a performance defect.

priorFinding.note: Not present in the prior index.

findings.whatWorks: ?view=app and ?view=compact are real and behave; the POST delta path works and saves 67%.
findings.requiredRepair: Two fixes, both small: correct the ARCHITECTURE.md arrow to POST /api/rankings/overrides?view=delta, and make /api/data reject an unknown view value with 400 rather than serving the default. The second is what stops the next wrong doc from costing bytes.
findings.rootCause: ARCHITECTURE.md was written from the intent ('the frontend gets a delta') rather than the route; nothing validates the view enum.

findings.title: The two prior audits scope different objects and neither is wrong; the 08-04 audit's registry is 372 commits stale and at least one Critical finding was fixed 6h44m after the SHA it read
findings.claimUnderTest: Two audits sit in docs/audits/ with nothing marking their relationship: 07-29 says 'Overall health: good, and better than the surrounding documentation suggested'; 08-04 says 'No — not at the decision layer ... Safe as a primary decision tool: 1'.
findings.observed: HYPOTHESIS TESTED: they scope the value SPINE versus the DECISION LAYER on top of it. FALSIFICATION CONDITION declared in advance: false if (F1) they assert opposite verdicts about the same named artefact with no scope difference, or (F2) the 08-04 negative case rests materially on defects inside the spine. EVALUATION — F1 not met: the 08-04 audit's own §1 concedes the 07-29 object verbatim ('a genuinely well-built spine: one canonical value, one blend path, a correctly-reasoned scoring-profile/league-key split, a real and largely-held rule against a frontend ranking engine') and scopes its verdict in the sentence itself ('No — NOT AT THE DECISION LAYER'). Its own registry entry PRIOR-A11-F12 checked CLAUDE.md's pipeline stage by stage and returned 'CONFIRMED CORRECT' on twelve consecutive spine claims, at Informational severity. F2 not met: six of its seven systemic problems are located above the spine (labellers, engines, missing-data defaults, monitoring, documentation); only #2 touches it, and #2 is an argument about the BENCHMARK grading the curves — which is the 07-29 audit's own stated open question. HYPOTHESIS SURVIVES. The single genuine head-to-head — the trade finder — resolves on chronology, not scope: the 08-04 audit read 9c5d972f (2026-08-04 06:32 UTC) and commit a62af217 'Fix the arbitrage finder dropping every IDP asset' landed at 13:16 UTC, 6h44m later and NOT an ancestor of the audited SHA. At HEAD the claim is refuted by runtime.

findings.userImpact: This is the finding that prevents wasted remediation. Without it a reader picks a winner between two correct audits, and either dismisses 173 open Critical/High decision-layer findings because 'the 07-29 audit said health is good', or re-fixes a trade-finder regression that was already fixed the same afternoon. The 08-04 registry's 531 findings are a claim set against a commit 372 behind HEAD, and the finder case proves at least one Critical entry was remediated in that window — in direct response to the audit.

priorFinding.note: My independent stage-by-stage pass over CLAUDE.md's Live Value Pipeline reached the same twelve verdicts as PRIOR-A11-F12 before I opened the index (constants, ordering, alpha, lambda, haircut, clamp scope, two-way ordering, Phase 3a/5.2b, weights all 1.0, default_weights unread). Separately REFUTES the 08-04 audit's problem-#4 finder claim at HEAD, and the refutation is chronological rather than a disagreement about facts.

findings.whatWorks: Both audits are unusually good at their own object, and both were honest about limits — the 07-29 audit lists inherited claims it disproved rather than dropping them, and the 08-04 audit states outright that it could not run pytest. What is missing is one scope line and one commit stamp in each header.
findings.rootCause: Two audits with different scopes filed to the same directory with no relationship metadata, and the newer one's SHA was not carried into its findings.

findings.title: 58 of 144 markdown documents are superseded, stale or self-declared untrustworthy, and only two of the 22 in docs/status/ say so
findings.claimUnderTest: HANDOFF.md designates CLAUDE.md 'The authority' and the repo's own documented top failure mode is docs-drift. Implicit claim: the surrounding 143 documents are a usable corpus.
findings.observed: 144 tracked markdown files outside node_modules/frontend/master-site-audit. Per-file disposition in supersession-list.csv: 81 KEEP, 48 ARCHIVE, 10 RETIRE, 5 REVIEW — 794,145 bytes (58 files) that should leave the working set. docs/status/ holds 22 files of which 20 have a latest internal date of 2026-04-28 or earlier and describe a pipeline retired at the 2026-04-20 Final Framework transition; exactly ONE carries a STALE banner and one 'superseded', so the other twenty read as current. UNIMPLEMENTED_BACKLOG.md (41,601 b) sits in the repo root beside CLAUDE.md with a header that says 'much of this file is already superseded' and 'the remaining entries were not re-verified one by one — treat them with the same suspicion', after two of its entries were found to be actively misreporting risk. docs/CLAUDE_SESSION_AUDIT_HANDOFF.md is 142,235 b — the largest document in the repo — and is a session-scoped handoff from 2026-07-31. Note git mtimes are useless for this: history was squashed on 2026-08-03, so every file shows the same date and only self-declared dates discriminate.

reproduction.expected: a corpus whose staleness is visible from the file
reproduction.actual: 144 docs; 20 of 22 in docs/status/ are >=3 months stale with no marker

numericProof.formula: archive + retire + review

findings.userImpact: This is the mechanism behind almost every other finding in this shard. A reader looking for the truth about the pipeline can land on docs/status/blueprint-source-of-truth.md (2026-03-14, no marker) or docs/BLUEPRINT_EXECUTION.md (STALE) and get a description of a system that was replaced four months ago, with no signal that anything is wrong. The repo's own 2026-08-04 audit named 'documentation mismatch' its single largest root-cause category; the corpus size is why.

priorFinding.note: The prior index carries individual doc-mismatch findings (82 records mention documentation or CLAUDE.md). None of them proposes a corpus-level disposition, which is what this audit needs in order to reduce the doc count rather than add to it.

findings.whatWorks: The repo is unusually honest when it does mark staleness — UNIMPLEMENTED_BACKLOG.md's header, final-framework-transition.md's 'superseded', and the struck-through corrections inside the backlog are all better practice than most codebases manage. The failure is that the honesty is applied to 1 file in 10.
findings.rootCause: No retirement step. Documents are added on completion and never removed, and the 2026-08-03 history squash destroyed the mtime signal that would otherwise expose age.
findings.requiredRepair: Execute supersession-list.csv: move the 48 ARCHIVE files to docs/archive/<period>/ with one INDEX.md each, delete the 10 RETIRE files, triage the 5 REVIEW. Then add a rule to HANDOFF.md: a doc that is not linked from HANDOFF.md within one release is archived. Net effect of this audit becomes -58 documents rather than +1.

findings.title: The mobile "compact" /api/data view is 13.0% LARGER than the desktop "array" view, so phones and low-memory devices are deliberately routed to the heavier payload
findings.claimUnderTest: server.py:3126-3128 — 'Mobile / slow-network view — prune ~20 audit + trust fields. ~90% byte reduction.'  frontend/lib/device-profile.js:84 — 'Mobile / slow network -> "compact"'.  frontend/app/api/dynasty-data/route.js:45 — 'mobile / slow-network callers ask for the compact (~90% smaller) view'.
findings.observed: compact serves 7,363,760 raw bytes; array serves 6,514,536; app serves 5,818,304; full serves 11,953,535.  compact is 849,224 bytes (+13.04%) LARGER than the view desktop asks for, and only 38.4% smaller than full — not 90%.  Mechanism, byte-accounted: view=array drops the legacy `players` dict entirely and ships playersArray only (6,132,969 b, 55 fields/row).  view=compact prunes 14 audit fields per row (55->41, playersArray 6,132,969 -> 3,659,280 b) but then ALSO ships the legacy `players` dict (3,336,826 b) — the same 1,092 rows encoded twice.  The per-row pruning is real and works; shipping both encodings more than cancels it.  Confirmed end-to-end in a real browser: desktop /rankings transferred 1,040,158 b / decoded 11,767,159 b; the same page at 390px transferred 1,135,662 b / decoded 12,553,077 b — mobile pays 95,504 more compressed bytes and 785,918 more decoded bytes.  isMobileProfile() also returns true for any device reporting navigator.deviceMemory <= 4, so budget laptops take the heavy path too.

reproduction.command: for v in '' '?view=app' '?view=array' '?view=compact'; do printf '%-16s raw=%s\n' "${v:-full}" $(curl -s -b /tmp/audit-cookies.txt -o /dev/null -w '%{size_download}' "http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/data$v"); done
reproduction.expected: compact <= array (a view named 'compact' and routed to the weakest devices should be the smallest non-degenerate view)

numericProof.formula: delta = compactTotalBytes - arrayTotalBytes ; pctLarger = 100*delta/arrayTotalBytes ; claimedReduction = 1 - compactTotalBytes/fullTotalBytes

findings.userImpact: A user on a phone or a 4 GB laptop downloads 95 KB more over the wire and parses 785 KB more JSON on every page load than the same user on a desktop, on a product whose stated design goal is 'mobile-friendly'. On a 3G connection the extra compressed bytes alone add roughly 0.5-1 s to first usable board.

blastRadius.note: 11 app pages call useDynastyData directly (grep -rln useDynastyData frontend/app | wc -l = 11); the finding's 13 counts pages reaching it through shared components. playersAffected is rows-double-encoded, not values-wrong.

priorFinding.note: PRIOR-A01-F17 established that desktop requests view=array and therefore has no legacy `players` dict, contradicting CLAUDE.md. This finding is the byte consequence on the OTHER side of that split: compact still carries the dict, which is exactly why it is bigger. PRIOR-A01-F08 is the correctness side of the same view (compact prunes four fields the rankings UI reads); the two are independent and both stand.

findings.whatWorks: The per-row compaction itself is correct and effective — 55 fields to 41, playersArray 6.13 MB to 3.66 MB. view=array's decision to drop the legacy dict is the right one. ETag + If-None-Match revalidation works on all views (304 in 3 ms, 0 bytes).
findings.rootCause: src/api/compact_view.py applies field pruning to BOTH `playersArray` and the legacy `players` dict, and the compact builder retains the dict, whereas the array builder deletes it. The compact view therefore ships two pruned encodings of the same 1,092 rows where array ships one unpruned encoding of one.
findings.requiredRepair: Delete the legacy `players` dict from the compact payload (it is what array already does) — that alone takes compact to ~4.03 MB, 38% below array and 66% below full, which is closer to the '~90%' the comments claim than anything shipping today. Then correct the three '~90% byte reduction' / '~90% smaller' comments to the measured figure.
findings.dependencies: Requires confirming no compact-view consumer reads the legacy dict; frontend/lib/dynasty-data.js::buildRows prefers playersArray when present, and view=array already proves the dict-free shape renders.

verification.reasoning: I tried to kill this three ways and could not. (1) The byte ordering reproduces exactly on today's stack: compact 7,365,099 > array 6,515,205 > app 5,818,973, a +849,894 b / +13.04% penalty for the view routed to phones — within the finding's 1,024 b tolerance of its stated 849,224. (2) The stated mechanism is right and I re-derived it independently: view=array ships playersArray only (55 fields/row) with the legacy `players` dict emptied, while view=compact ships a pruned playersArray (41 fields/row) AND a pruned legacy `players` dict (1,092 keys, 50 fields/row, 3.61 MB) — the same rows encoded twice, which more than cancels a real and correct per-row pruning. (3) The path is live, not theoretical: frontend/lib/dynasty-data.js:1495 calls device-profile.preferredDataView(), which returns 'compact' for isMobileProfile() || isSlowNetwork() (device-profile.js:103-108), and a 390x844 browser under the sanctioned interception topology genuinely issued /api/dynasty-data?view=compact and pulled 7,365,099 decoded bytes for the identical 230-row board the 1500px browser rendered from 6,515,205. Over the wire the penalty is +97,268 gzipped bytes. The three '~90% byte reduction' / '~90% smaller' comments (server.py:3126-3128, device-profile.js:82-90, frontend/app/api/dynasty-data/route.js:45, plus src/api/compact_view.py:3-5 '~4MB to ~500KB') are all wrong by roughly an order of magnitude — measured reduction vs full is 38.4%. Not a harness artifact, not fixed at HEAD (ba9f348b), not dead code. Severity: I considered downgrading to P2 since no number is wrong and compact is still 38% below the full view, but the finding did not claim P0 and P1 is defensible for a live inversion of an explicit design decision on every mobile page load; I have no evidence-based grounds to move it. One category correction only: playersAffected 1,092 means 'rows duplicated in the payload', not 'players whose value is wrong' — no value is affected.
verification.whatWouldSettleIt: Already settled. The fix is one line of parity with the array builder — drop the legacy `players` dict from the compact payload — after confirming no compact consumer reads it; buildRows already prefers playersArray and view=array proves the dict-free shape renders (230 rows at both viewports above).

findings.title: AppShell fetches the full multi-megabyte player contract on EVERY private page — including a 404 page and pages that never render a player row
findings.claimUnderTest: CLAUDE.md 'Performance Rules' — 'Reduce blocking work on initial load', 'Eliminate duplicated calculations, repeated fetches, oversized payloads'. AppShell.jsx:33 declares exactly one exemption from the private data fetch, PUBLIC_ONLY_ROUTE_PREFIXES = ['/league'], and that exemption exists for a SECURITY reason (leaking private rankings to public visitors), not a performance one.
findings.observed: Measured in a real browser through request interception, 13 of the 14 pages probed issue GET /api/dynasty-data?view=array|compact and decode 11.7-13.1 MB.  The only page that does not is /league, which is exempt for security.  Pages that fetch the whole 1,092-row board while rendering none of it: /news (12,533,315 b decoded), /bdvm (12,488,678), /market/sharp-roster-percentage (12,481,120), /league-comparison (12,560,784), /waivers (12,578,490), /settings (12,505,629).  /terminal — which is a Next 404, 'This page could not be found.' — still decodes 12,481,320 bytes.  The fetch is unconditional in PrivateAppShell (AppShell.jsx:61) because global search and the player popup want `rows`; the actual index those two need is name + id + position + value, roughly 90 KB for 1,092 rows.

reproduction.command: PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=/opt/pw-browsers .venv/bin/python docs/master-site-audit/evidence/W26/w26_probe.py /tmp/out.json   # then: jq '.[]|select(.viewport=="mobile")|{route,api:.apiUnique,decoded:.timing.decodedBytes}' /tmp/out.json
reproduction.expected: pages with no player board (/news, /bdvm, /league-comparison, /market/*, and a 404) do not download the player board
reproduction.actual: all of them download 12.4-12.6 MB decoded

numericProof.formula: wastedDecodedBytes_per_page_without_a_board = decodedBytes - (bytes actually rendered); for /terminal (a 404) the rendered board bytes are 0

findings.userImpact: Opening /news to read three headlines, or /bdvm to see a 'no snapshot yet' message, costs the user a full board download and JSON parse. On mobile this is the dominant cost of every navigation in the app and it is paid before anything on the page can render its own data. A mistyped URL that lands on the 404 page costs 1.0 MB over the wire.

blastRadius.note: routesAffected 1: only /api/dynasty-data is the shell fetch; /api/rankings/overrides?view=delta rides the same code path but is user-state-conditional. playersAffected is not a meaningful axis for a payload-size finding — the correct cost axis is 671,811 b wire / 6,515,205 b decoded per COLD load of a board-less page, and 0 additional bytes per in-session navigation.

priorFinding.note: No prior finding covers the app-shell-level unconditional contract fetch. PRIOR-A01-F17 and PRIOR-A01-F08 concern which VIEW is fetched, not that it is fetched everywhere.

findings.whatWorks: The fetch itself is well engineered: single request per page, zero duplicate URLs measured across all 28 page/viewport combinations, ETag revalidation with 304 support, gzip, and a stream-through Next bridge with an idle-abort timeout. The /league security exemption is correctly implemented and correctly motivated.
findings.rootCause: AppShell.jsx:61 calls useDynastyData() unconditionally in PrivateAppShell. The only gate (isPublicOnlyRoute) was added for data-leak reasons; no route-level gate exists for 'this page has no board'.
findings.requiredRepair: Either (a) split useDynastyData into a lightweight search-index fetch (name/playerId/position/rankDerivedValue) that AppShell always makes and a full-board fetch that only board-rendering pages opt into, or (b) invert the gate so pages declare `needsBoard` and AppShell defers the full fetch until one does. Option (a) preserves global search on every page at ~1.5% of the current bytes.
findings.dependencies: Needs a new lightweight backend view (or reuse of ?view=startup narrowed further). Interacts with W26-F001 — fix that first so whichever view remains is the smallest.

verification.reasoning: The core mechanism is confirmed: AppShell.jsx:33-75 gates the private data fetch on exactly one prefix list (PUBLIC_ONLY_ROUTE_PREFIXES = ['/league'], added for data-leak reasons), so PrivateAppShell calls useDynastyData() on every other route including board-less pages and Next's not-found — I re-measured a cold /news hard load and it does fetch /api/dynasty-data?view=array. Three parts of the finding do not survive re-measurement. (1) Attribution: 'decode 11.7-13.1 MB' is the sum of decodedBodySize over ALL resource entries (w26_probe.py:245), not the contract. The player contract is 6,515,205 b decoded / 671,811 b on the wire. Of the rest, 3,897,831 b decoded / 369,861 b wire is a SECOND request, POST /api/rankings/overrides?view=delta, and that one is conditional on the user having customized source weights (dynasty-data.js:2017-2035 — a default user takes the !customized branch and never posts it). The remaining ~1.3 MB decoded is app JS/CSS that any page must load. So the title's 'fetches the full multi-megabyte player contract' is right, but 'costs 12.5 MB' is not the contract's cost, and the numericProof's formula (whole-page decodedBytes minus rendered board = waste) charges the Next bundle to this defect. (2) 'On mobile this is the dominant cost of every navigation in the app' is false. AppShell lives in the root layout and does not remount on client-side navigation, and dynasty-data.js:1413-1440 adds a module-level cache with a 30s TTL plus in-flight dedupe. Measured: navigating /rankings -> /news by clicking the nav link produced exactly ONE /api/dynasty-data request in total. The original probe's per-page cost is an artifact of probing each route with a fresh page.goto. (3) The flagship example is a Next 404 (/terminal has no directory under frontend/app), so 'a mistyped URL costs 1.0 MB' is true of a cold context only, and ~0.67 MB of that is the contract. What is left is a real but ordinary perf inefficiency: a cold entry on a board-less page pays ~672 KB over the wire and a 6.5 MB JSON parse it does not use, to keep global search and the player popup working. No number a user acts on is wrong, ETag/304 revalidation and the module cache bound the repeat cost, and the finding itself credits both. P2, not P1.
verification.whatWouldSettleIt: A cold-cache mobile trace of the first entry into the app (which is the one load that genuinely pays it) with the contract fetch isolated from the bundle, plus a measurement of the >30s-TTL revalidation path — if that returns 304 with a near-zero body, the per-navigation cost is confirmed as ~0 and the finding is strictly a first-paint cost.

findings.title: /draft downloads the full 11.95 MB /api/data contract to read a 46.8 KB list of 12 team names, from three separate call sites, two of them with cache: "no-store"
findings.claimUnderTest: server.py:8324-8329 records that /api/draft-capital was already fixed once for exactly this class of problem — '/draft calling it three times per page load'. The contract fetch on the same page was not covered by that fix.
findings.observed: /draft issues BOTH `/api/data?leagueKey=dynasty_main` (no `view` param, so the backend serves the FULL 11,953,535-byte contract) AND `/api/dynasty-data?view=array` (6,514,536 b), plus `/api/data` bare from a third call site. Browser-measured totals for /draft: desktop decoded 23,849,422 b / transferred 2,216,644 b; mobile decoded 24,571,176 b / transferred 2,312,148 b — roughly double every other page in the app. All three /api/data call sites consume only `data.sleeper.teams`, which is 46,792 bytes of the 11,953,535 served — 0.39%. Two of the three pass `cache: "no-store"`, which defeats both the browser HTTP cache and the ETag/304 path the backend already implements, so the bytes are re-fetched on every mount and every sync-preview click.

reproduction.command: curl -s -b /tmp/audit-cookies.txt 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/data?leagueKey=dynasty_main' -o /tmp/f.json && python3 -c "import json,os;d=json.load(open('/tmp/f.json'));print('served',os.path.getsize('/tmp/f.json'),'sleeper.teams',len(json.dumps(d['sleeper']['teams'])),'teams',len(d['sleeper']['teams']))"
reproduction.expected: the page fetches roughly the bytes it consumes
reproduction.actual: served 11953535  sleeper.teams 46792  teams 12

numericProof.formula: utilisation = sleeperTeamsBytes / fullContractBytes

findings.userImpact: Opening the live draft board — the one page a user loads under time pressure, mid-auction, often on a phone on venue wifi — costs twice the bytes of any other page. Clicking 'Sync rookies' re-downloads the full 11.95 MB contract again because that call site is cache:no-store.

blastRadius.note: routesAffected recounted to 1: /api/data and /api/data?leagueKey=dynasty_main are the same route, and /api/dynasty-data?view=array is fetched by /rankings too — it is not part of the /draft-specific excess. playersAffected recounted to 0 (payload weight, not a value defect). The per-load excess is the single mount-time fetch: 1,180,466 b transferred / ~11,908,082 b decoded to obtain 46,792 b of team names.

priorFinding.note: PRIOR-A00-* findings on /draft concern bid arithmetic, not payload. The /api/draft-capital triple-fetch on this page was fixed previously (server.py:8324); the contract triple-fetch beside it was not.

findings.whatWorks: The parallelisation in fetchSyncPreview (Promise.all over /api/data and /api/draft-capital) is correct — those two are genuinely independent and are not serialised. The cancellation guard on the mount effect is correct.
findings.rootCause: Three call sites want `sleeper.teams` and there is no narrow endpoint that serves it, so each reaches for the whole contract. None passes a `view` param, so each gets the widest view the backend has.
findings.requiredRepair: Add `?view=startup` (or a new teams-only view) to the three call sites — that alone halves the cost — and hoist the three fetches into one memoised call keyed on selectedLeagueKey. Drop `cache: "no-store"` so the backend's existing ETag/304 does its job. Best fix: serve `sleeper.teams` from the existing /api/leagues response, which already carries per-league roster settings and would make the contract fetch unnecessary here.

verification.reasoning: The load-path core survives and I measured it independently. On a real /draft mount the page issues `/api/data?leagueKey=dynasty_main` and gets a 200 whose gzipped content-length is 1,180,466 (≈11.95 MB decoded), and the only field the mount-time call site consumes is `data.sleeper.teams` — 46,792 bytes, 0.39% (frontend/app/draft/page.jsx:3932-3937, `cache: "no-store"`, then `const teams = data?.sleeper?.teams || []`). The backend already serves etag + `cache-control: private, max-age=30` on that route, so `no-store` does defeat a working 304 path. /draft measured ≈2.1x /rankings in both decoded and transferred bytes, which corroborates the author's 'roughly double every other page'. My first measurement pass appeared to refute the whole finding (total decoded 11.9 MB, no /api/data in the response log) — that was my own instrumentation artifact: Chrome evicts response bodies over its buffer, `resp.body()` throws 'Request content was evicted', and my handler was swallowing it. Header-level accounting recovered it. So the finding is not killed. Three things are overstated and one is simply wrong. (1) WRONG: 'All three /api/data call sites consume only data.sleeper.teams ... 0.39%'. Call site 2 — fetchSyncPreview at page.jsx:4201-4224 — consumes `data.playersArray` (`setAllPlayersArray(pa)`, page.jsx:4233), which is 6,673,553 of the 11,954,874 bytes and is the entire point of that fetch. Its waste is the duplicated legacy `players` dict (5,914,408 b), not 99.6% of the payload. Two of three call sites consume only teams, not three. (2) OVERSTATED: 'from three separate call sites' on page load. Measured: exactly ONE completed /api/data response per load. Call site 2 is click-gated ('Sync rookies'); call site 3 (page.jsx:4484-4487) is gated on `allPlayersArray` being set, i.e. post-sync, and uses `cache: "force-cache"`, not no-store. The claimUnderTest analogy to the prior '/draft calling it three times per page load' fix therefore does not transfer — the per-load count is 1. (3) OVERSTATED: the bare `/api/data` is attributed to 'a third call site'. It comes from call site 1 itself, whose URL expression is bare until `selectedLeagueKey` resolves; the bare request is superseded and never lands. (4) BLAST RADIUS: playersAffected 1092 is meaningless here — no player value is wrong; this is a payload-weight finding. Priority held at P1, not lowered: the surviving defect (1.18 MB gzipped / ~11.95 MB parsed, on mount, on the app's most time-critical page, to read 12 team names, with the backend's own ETag deliberately bypassed) is a genuine violation of this repo's stated performance rules. Rescoped for claim scope, not severity.
verification.whatWouldSettleIt: Point page.jsx:3930 at a narrow view (`/api/data?view=startup`, or serve sleeper.teams from /api/leagues, which /draft already fetches at 840 b) and drop `cache: "no-store"`; then re-run the header-level Playwright accounting above and /draft's transferred total should fall from ≈2.25 MB to ≈1.07 MB, matching /rankings. Note the measurement must read `content-length` from the response headers — `resp.body()` throws 'Request content was evicted' on this payload and silently under-reports by 11.9 MB, which is what nearly overturned this finding.

findings.title: GET /api/bdvm/roster spends 48 seconds on nflverse downloads that the very next function call discards, because the code already knows there is no projection snapshot before it starts fetching
findings.claimUnderTest: src/api/bdvm_api.py module docstring — 'Thin, cached bridge... Player context (nflverse id map + career loads) and the season schedule are fetched lazily'. AUDIT_PROTOCOL pre-declares 'data/bdvm/ does not exist -> Blocked by data', so the 'no snapshot' ANSWER is not the finding; the 48 seconds spent producing it is.
findings.observed: bdvm_api.py:177 computes `snapshot = latest_snapshot_path(season)` and gets None. On a cache miss it nonetheless calls `_context_for(season)` (line 200) and `_schedule_for(season)` (line 201) before `run_valuation`. run_valuation returns `no_projection_snapshot` at service.py:305 — before it reads `context` (first used line 338/453) or `schedule_weeks` (line 622). Every byte fetched is discarded. Measured cost: the shared route probe recorded 47,994 ms for a 310-byte response on the cold path; re-run in a fresh process against an already-warm nfl_data disk cache the same two calls still cost 8.69 s (schedule 1.27 s, context 7.41 s, 23,934 context players built and thrown away). The 48 s figure is the cold cost of downloading the nflverse id map (24.7 MB), six seasons of weekly stats (357.4 MB) and six seasons of snap counts (51.4 MB). Sibling routes /api/bdvm/values and /api/bdvm/trades measured 6 ms and 5 ms in the same probe run purely because /api/bdvm/roster (alphabetically first) had already paid and warmed the per-process _context_cache / _schedule_cache. schedule.py additionally retries a second 60 s-timeout URL on failure, so the schedule leg alone can block 120 s.

reproduction.command: .venv/bin/python -c "import time;from src.bdvm.projections import latest_snapshot_path;from src.bdvm.actuals import nfl_projection_season;s=nfl_projection_season();print('snapshot',latest_snapshot_path(s));t=time.time();from src.bdvm.schedule import fetch_team_weeks;fetch_team_weeks(s);a=time.time()-t;t=time.time();from src.bdvm.context import fetch_and_build_context;c=fetch_and_build_context(s);print('schedule_s',round(a,2),'context_s',round(time.time()-t,2),'players',len(c))"
reproduction.expected: 0 s — with snapshot None the engine has nothing to value
reproduction.actual: snapshot None ; schedule_s 1.27 ; context_s 7.41 ; players 23934  (47,994 ms on a cold nfl_data cache)

numericProof.formula: wastedSeconds = scheduleSeconds + contextSeconds, given latest_snapshot_path(season) is None at bdvm_api.py:177 and run_valuation returns at service.py:305 before either value is read

findings.userImpact: The first user to open /bdvm after any process restart waits 48 seconds for a message that says 'no projection snapshot' — information the server had in under a millisecond. In production WITH a snapshot the same 48 s is still paid on the first request after every deploy, and it holds an anyio threadpool worker (of 40) for the whole duration.

priorFinding.note: PRIOR-A15-F16 flagged that get_bdvm_values' cache key contains id(contract), a reusable CPython address — I confirm that line is still present (bdvm_api.py:180). This finding is a different defect in the same function: the ordering of the snapshot check against the two network fetches.

findings.whatWorks: The refusal itself is exemplary — the engine returns status no_projection_snapshot with an actionable message and does not fabricate projections, exactly as the module contract promises. The LRU sizing rationale (_VALUES_CACHE_MAX=4, bdvm_api.py:36-40) is well reasoned. The 'failed actuals fetch is returned but never memoized' rule (lines 143-153) is a genuinely good cache-poisoning guard.
findings.rootCause: The snapshot existence check lives inside run_valuation (service.py:303) while the two expensive enrichment fetches live in the caller (bdvm_api.py:200-201). The caller already computes the same snapshot path at line 177 for its cache key, so it has the information it needs to skip.
findings.requiredRepair: Three lines: after `snapshot = latest_snapshot_path(season)` at bdvm_api.py:177, if snapshot is None pass `context={}` and `schedule_weeks=None` straight through instead of calling _context_for / _schedule_for. Separately, drop schedule.py's second 60 s-timeout attempt to a much shorter budget — a 120 s worst case on an optional enrichment is not a sane bound for a request path.

findings.title: Three of the slowest cold paths have no stampede protection: concurrent misses each run the full multi-second build
findings.claimUnderTest: The repo demonstrably knows this pattern: server.py implements per-key asyncio single-flight for _OVERLAY_RESPONSE_CACHE (line 2960), _OVERRIDES_RESPONSE_CACHE (line 3011), _DRAFT_CAPITAL_CACHE (line 8375) and _heavy_section_cache (line 8758), and src/api/sleeper_overlay.py:_BUILD_LOCKS documents 'before these locks concurrent expirees each launched their own storm'.
findings.observed: Four caches on the slowest measured routes hold their lock only across the dict get/put, never across the build.  (1) bdvm_api._context_for / _schedule_for release _aux_lock before fetching, so N concurrent cold /api/bdvm/* requests each launch a full nflverse download (433 MB per attempt, measured 47,994 ms).  (2) bdvm_api.get_bdvm_values releases _lock at line 197 and re-acquires at 214, so N concurrent misses each run run_valuation.  (3) league_comparison.service.build_comparison has a 7-day DISK cache and no lock at all — cold cost measured 26,577 ms in the route probe; N concurrent cold requests each load every nflverse season and recompute.  (4) gameplan.get_league_bundle holds _CACHE_LOCK only around the dict lookup while its own docstring says 'only the ~1.35 s solve is cached'.

reproduction.command: grep -n 'with _aux_lock' -A3 src/api/bdvm_api.py | sed -n '1,20p'   # lock released before the fetch on lines 64-70 and 80-86; compare server.py:2958-2996 which holds an asyncio.Lock across the whole encode
reproduction.expected: the build runs inside the lock, or a per-key single-flight lock exists
reproduction.actual: lock scope covers only the dict access; the multi-second build runs unlocked

numericProof.formula: worst-case work on a cold cache = N * coldMs instead of 1 * coldMs; with bdvm at 47,994 ms and 40 threadpool workers, 40 concurrent cold /api/bdvm/* requests saturate the entire pool for ~48 s

findings.userImpact: A cold restart plus a handful of simultaneous users (or one user with several tabs) multiplies the 48 s / 27 s cold costs instead of sharing them, and can occupy every threadpool worker so unrelated endpoints queue behind it.

priorFinding.note: No prior finding covers stampede protection. Rated medium rather than high because I could not safely generate concurrent cold misses under the audit's read-only rule (it would force real outbound nflverse fetches); the claim rests on the lock scope in source plus the measured single-request cold costs.

findings.whatWorks: Four other caches in this codebase get this exactly right, with the reasoning written down: _OVERLAY_RESPONSE_CACHE / _OVERRIDES_RESPONSE_CACHE (per-key asyncio.Lock, re-check inside the lock, held locks preserved across eviction), _DRAFT_CAPITAL_CACHE (per-league asyncio.Lock with post-wait re-check), _heavy_section_cache (waiters block on the loop, not in the threadpool, so they do not hold worker tokens hostage), and sleeper_overlay._BUILD_LOCKS. The public-league cache goes further with stale-while-revalidate, a suppression flag on the background refresh thread, and hit/miss/stale counters.
findings.rootCause: These four caches were written as plain memoisation ('check dict, else compute, else store') without adopting the single-flight pattern the same repo uses elsewhere.
findings.requiredRepair: Port the existing pattern: a per-key lock dict, acquire it on miss, re-check inside, compute, store, release. For bdvm_api use threading.Lock (the work runs in a threadpool worker); for league_comparison the same; for gameplan widen _CACHE_LOCK to cover the solve or add a per-league build lock.

findings.title: GET /api/player/{id}/realized re-reads and re-parses a 61.7 MB JSON file and linearly scans 19,421 rows on every single request, with no in-process memoisation
findings.claimUnderTest: src/nfl_data/cache.py module docstring — 'We don't want to hammer nflverse on every request... so every ingest call goes through this cache.' The cache prevents network hammering; it does not prevent disk-and-CPU hammering, and nothing above it memoises.
findings.observed: The handler calls `_ing.fetch_weekly_stats([2025, 2026])` per request. That resolves to a DISK-only TTL cache — `cache.get()` does `json.loads(data_path.read_text())` with no in-process layer — so every call re-reads and re-parses the 61,706,838-byte cache entry for key `weekly_stats:2025,2026` and materialises 19,421 dict rows. The handler then filters those 19,421 rows with a Python list comprehension to find one player's GSIS id. Measured directly: 0.762 s for the first fetch and 0.745 s for an immediately-repeated fetch in the same process — no memoisation at any level. End-to-end route latency, repeated 5x: 5.179 s (cold) then 1.136 / 0.954 / 0.915 / 0.840 s. The steady state is ~0.8 s of pure server CPU per player popup. PlayerPopup fires this on every popup open (client-side 30-minute cache is per playerId only), so a user browsing 20 players costs ~16 s of server CPU and ~1.2 GB of JSON parsing.

reproduction.command: .venv/bin/python -c "import time;from src.nfl_data import ingest;t=time.time();r=ingest.fetch_weekly_stats([2025,2026]);print('rows',len(r),'first_s',round(time.time()-t,3));t=time.time();ingest.fetch_weekly_stats([2025,2026]);print('second_s',round(time.time()-t,3))" ; for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do curl -s -o /dev/null -b /tmp/audit-cookies.txt -w '%{time_total}\n' 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/player/4046/realized'; done
reproduction.expected: second in-process fetch is ~0 s (memoised); route steady state well under 100 ms
reproduction.actual: rows 19421 first_s 0.762 second_s 0.745 ; route steady state 0.79-0.95 s

numericProof.formula: serverSecondsPerSession = routeSteadyStateSeconds * popupsPerBrowsingSession ; bytesParsedPerSession = cacheFileBytes * popupsPerBrowsingSession

findings.userImpact: Every player popup that reaches the realized-points section stalls ~0.8 s server-side, and the cost is per-player rather than per-session, so it scales linearly with browsing. Under concurrent users each request also allocates ~60 MB of transient Python objects.

priorFinding.note: PRIOR-A21-F16 and PRIOR-A22-F02 both concern the CORRECTNESS of this route (wrong league's scoring; IDP players return zero weeks). Neither touches the per-request 61.7 MB re-parse. Independent.

findings.whatWorks: The client-side cache in PlayerPopup (_realizedCache, 30-minute TTL keyed by sleeperId, with negative caching on failure) is correct and does real work. The handler's row-filter comment documenting the player_id vs player_id_gsis bug is exactly the kind of note that prevents a regression.
findings.rootCause: src/nfl_data/cache.py is a disk-only TTL cache with no in-process layer, and no caller adds one. A request-scoped or process-scoped memo of the parsed rows was never introduced because the cache's docstring frames the problem as network hammering only.
findings.requiredRepair: Add an in-process memo above the disk cache keyed on (cache key, file mtime_ns) so the parse happens once per process per refresh. Separately, build a GSIS-id index once instead of a 19,421-row linear scan per player — that turns the filter from O(n) per request into O(1).

findings.title: The nfl_data disk cache has no last-known-good fallback, no size bound (590 MB today), and stores three byte-identical copies of the same 61.7 MB file under three keys
findings.claimUnderTest: cache.py:1-15 — 'TTL file cache for NFL data pulls... every ingest call goes through this cache.' ingest.py:315-330 — on a stale entry the fetch is retried and, if it returns None, `return []` — the still-present, still-parseable cached file is not consulted.
findings.observed: Three distinct defects in one cache.  (a) NO LAST-KNOWN-GOOD: cache.get() returns None the instant `(now - fetched_at) > ttl_seconds` (line 84) and every ingest wrapper then returns [] if the refetch fails. A 24h+1s-old, perfectly usable 61.7 MB file on disk is ignored, so a transient nflverse outage turns /api/player/{id}/realized into a 200 with `reason: "no_stats_available"` and every ROS/BDVM consumer into an empty result — from full data to no data with no intermediate degradation.  (b) NO SIZE BOUND: there is no prune, no LRU, no total-bytes cap — the only unlink() calls are for corrupt entries and explicit evict(key). Measured today: 590 MB across 7 entries, the largest a single 357,376,944-byte JSON.  (c) DUPLICATE STORAGE: keys are the sorted YEAR LIST, so `weekly_stats:2025` and `weekly_stats:2025,2026` are md5-identical (071b2583...) because 2026 has no rows yet; and `weekly_def_stats:2025` is the SAME md5 again, because nflverse_direct maps both `weekly_stats` and `weekly_defensive_stats` to one unified URL (documented at nflverse_direct.py:82-83). That is 185,120,514 bytes — 31% of the cache — holding three copies of one file.

reproduction.command: cd data/nfl_data_cache && for f in *.meta.json; do d=${f%.meta.json}.json; k=$(python3 -c "import json;print(json.load(open('$f'))['key'])"); echo "$(md5sum $d|cut -c1-32) $(stat -c%s $d) $k"; done | sort ; du -sh data/nfl_data_cache
reproduction.expected: distinct keys hold distinct content; total cache size bounded
reproduction.actual: 071b2583811fc9a3dbad5ad156a4be9c appears for weekly_def_stats:2025, weekly_stats:2025 and weekly_stats:2025,2026 (61,706,838 b each); total 590M

numericProof.formula: wastedBytes = duplicatedEntryBytes * (duplicateCopies - 1)

findings.userImpact: On the (b) axis, an unattended production box accumulates nflverse snapshots until the disk fills, at which point cache.put() raises and the ingest flow breaks. On the (a) axis, the day nflverse is briefly unreachable after a TTL expiry, several surfaces flip from correct data to honest-but-empty in one step, when a 25-hour-old snapshot would have been almost exactly as good.

priorFinding.note: No prior finding covers the nfl_data cache layer itself.

findings.whatWorks: Atomic-ish writes (tempfile + rename) are correct and prevent a crashed process from wedging the cache. Corrupt-entry self-eviction on both the meta and data paths is correct. JSON rather than pickle for portability is the right call and is justified in the docstring. The put() failure path deliberately swallows so a full disk does not kill ingest.
findings.rootCause: cache.get() implements a hard TTL with no stale tier, cache.put() implements no accounting, and cache keys are derived from the caller's argument list rather than from the underlying resource, so two callers requesting overlapping year ranges of one file get separate full copies.
findings.requiredRepair: (a) Add a `stale_ok` return path — get() returns (value, is_stale) and ingest wrappers serve stale on refetch failure with a staleness stamp on the payload, so the honest-empty state is reserved for 'we have never had this'. (b) Add a total-bytes budget with oldest-first eviction, checked in put(). (c) Key weekly stats per SEASON, not per year-list, and dedupe the offense/defense entries onto the single unified file the URL map already points both at.

findings.title: An unauthenticated caller can force /api/draft-capital's full workbook+KTC+Sleeper rebuild every 300 s, and a failing KTC live fetch is never negative-cached so the cost recurs forever
findings.claimUnderTest: server.py:8323-8336 — 'This endpoint used to run ~4s of synchronous work... Cache: key = league key; TTL = 300s'. The cache is real; what is not addressed is who is allowed to miss it and what a failing upstream costs.
findings.observed: Two coupled defects.  (a) ANONYMOUS COLD BUILD: /api/draft-capital returns 200 to an unauthenticated caller (redacted, `rookieBoardRedacted: true`), but redaction happens per-response AFTER the build. So an anon client that polls every 5 minutes forces the full openpyxl workbook parse + KTC live fetch + up to six Sleeper calls on every TTL expiry. Measured anonymously with no cookie: 2.692 s, then 0.003 s, 0.004 s (cache hit) — and the shared route probe caught the genuinely cold first call at 13,188 ms.  (b) NO NEGATIVE CACHING ON KTC: `_get_ktc_rookies()` (server.py:7113) returns the 6h cache when fresh, else calls `_fetch_ktc_rookies_live()` (15 s urlopen timeout). On failure it falls through to `_parse_csv_rookies()` and returns those rows WITHOUT writing `_ktc_cache["fetched_at"]`. The failure is therefore never remembered: every subsequent draft-capital cache miss re-attempts the failing live scrape. That is the 2.692 s I measured — the KTC attempt timing out, once per 300 s, forever, in a production where KTC is blocked or rate-limiting.

reproduction.command: for i in 1 2 3; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'anon %{http_code} %{size_download}b %{time_total}s\n' 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/draft-capital'; done   # no cookie jar
reproduction.expected: anonymous callers cannot trigger a multi-second server-side build; a failing upstream is remembered

numericProof.formula: forcedRebuildsPerDayPerLeague = secondsPerDay / draftCapitalTtlSeconds ; serverSecondsPerDay = forcedRebuildsPerDayPerLeague * anonColdSeconds

findings.userImpact: On a public deployment this is a free amplification vector: 288 forced rebuilds per day per league from an unauthenticated client, each holding a threadpool worker for 2.7-13.2 s. For the legitimate user, every /draft load that lands just after a TTL expiry pays the failing-KTC timeout instead of the 3 ms cache hit.

priorFinding.note: PRIOR-A00-F04 concerns the CORRECTNESS of the Sleeper-derived draft-capital board (fabricated pick values). This is the ingest/caching axis of the same endpoint and is independent of it. The anonymous 200 itself may be intentional public-board behaviour — the finding is the uncached COST behind it, not the exposure.

findings.whatWorks: The per-league asyncio single-flight lock with a post-wait re-check (server.py:8375-8394) is correct and does prevent the /draft triple-fetch from fanning out. Redacting on a per-response copy rather than mutating the cached object (documented at 8337-8340) is exactly right and avoids a nasty cross-viewer leak. `ktcSource: "csv"` is honestly stamped on the response so a consumer can tell the live fetch failed.
findings.rootCause: The 300 s TTL bounds staleness but not who may pay to refill it, and `_get_ktc_rookies` treats a failed live fetch as 'try again next time' rather than as a fact worth caching.
findings.requiredRepair: On live-fetch failure, stamp `_ktc_cache` with the CSV rows and a shortened `fetched_at` (e.g. 15-minute backoff) so the failure is remembered — the CSV fallback is already the answer, so caching it costs nothing. Separately, serve anonymous callers only from an existing cache entry and return the last-known-good (or 503) rather than letting them trigger a build.

findings.title: /api/bdvm/* and /api/valuation/league-adjusted send no Cache-Control and no ETag, so an expensive league-scoped payload is re-requested and re-sent on every navigation
findings.claimUnderTest: Every other comparable route on this server sets an explicit policy: /api/data 'private, max-age=30, stale-while-revalidate=300' with an ETag; /api/terminal 'private, max-age=30, stale-while-revalidate=120'; /api/news 'public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=180'; /api/public/league 'public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300'; /api/draft-capital 'private, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300'; /api/league-comparison 'private, max-age=300, stale-while-revalidate=3600'.
findings.observed: curl -D- shows no cache-control, no etag and no age header on /api/bdvm/values or /api/valuation/league-adjusted. /api/valuation/league-adjusted is a 48,555-byte league-scoped payload measured at 7,267 ms cold and 60-77 ms warm; /api/bdvm/values is up to 792 b today but is the full fundamental board once a snapshot exists. With no directive the browser applies heuristic freshness (or none), so every navigation to /rankings re-requests the overlay and the server re-serialises it.

reproduction.command: for r in /api/data /api/terminal /api/news /api/bdvm/values /api/valuation/league-adjusted; do echo "-- $r"; curl -s -D- -o /dev/null -b /tmp/audit-cookies.txt "http://127.0.0.1:8000$r" | grep -i '^cache-control\|^etag'; done
reproduction.expected: every route states a caching policy
reproduction.actual: /api/data, /api/terminal, /api/news all print cache-control; /api/bdvm/values and /api/valuation/league-adjusted print nothing

numericProof.formula: bytes re-sent per navigation with no policy = valuationOverlayBytes (vs 0 on a 304)

findings.userImpact: Switching the /rankings valuation toggle back and forth, or navigating between board pages, re-downloads and re-serialises the league-adjusted overlay each time rather than revalidating for free.

priorFinding.note: No prior finding covers HTTP cache headers.

findings.whatWorks: The six routes that DO set a policy set a sensible one, and /api/data additionally implements ETag + If-None-Match with a working 304 (verified: 304 in 3.1 ms, 0 bytes) and Vary: Accept-Encoding. The client-side compensation is also real — useTerminal keys its cache on valuationMode, which is the right key.
findings.rootCause: These handlers return JSONResponse(content=...) without a headers argument, unlike their peers.
findings.requiredRepair: Add `headers={"Cache-Control": "private, max-age=30, stale-while-revalidate=300"}` plus an ETag over the serialised body, matching /api/data. Both payloads are already versioned (paramSetId / configHash / asOf on bdvm; league factors stamp on the overlay), so a content ETag is trivially derivable.
findings.dependencies: Note a cosmetic defect in the same area: /api/data emits `Vary: Accept-Encoding, Accept-Encoding` (duplicated token) because the header is set in two places.

findings.title: The home page's Top Movers panel prints "No qualifying movers in this window" and a "Rank deltas vs. 30d ago" subtitle when the backend has told it there are ZERO days of history — an empty state that reads as a market fact
findings.claimUnderTest: server.py:3385-3386 documents the distinction explicitly: "`window` is the span we ACTUALLY measured, not the span that was asked for — `windowRequested` echoes the request." The backend deliberately publishes `window`, `windowRequested` and `historyDepthDays` so a client can tell 'nothing moved' from 'nothing measured'. The frontend reads none of the three.
findings.observed: GET /api/movers returns {"window":0,"windowRequested":14,"historyDepthDays":0,"threshold":15,"asOf":null,"risers":[],"fallers":[]}. `historyDepthDays: 0` and `asOf: null` mean the platform holds a single rank snapshot, so no delta over any window is computable. MoversPanel.jsx:201 and :217 branch only on `risers.length === 0` / `fallers.length === 0` and render 'No qualifying movers in this window.' under headings 'Risers — sell-high candidates' and 'Fallers — buy-low candidates', with the panel subtitle asserting 'Rank deltas vs. 30d ago · click a row for source breakdown'. A 30-day rank delta was never computed. MarketTicker.jsx:126 compounds it: 'Market quiet in my roster — fewer than 3 moves since last update.' Both sentences state a property of the MARKET; the true property is of our DATA. Captured verbatim from the rendered page.

reproduction.command: curl -s -b /tmp/audit-cookies.txt 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/movers' ; echo ; PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=/opt/pw-browsers .venv/bin/python docs/master-site-audit/evidence/W26/w26_probe.py /tmp/o.json && python3 -c "import json;print([r['dom']['bodyText'] for r in json.load(open('/tmp/o.json')) if r['route']=='/' and r['viewport']=='desktop'][0][:1200])"
reproduction.expected: the panel says it has no rank history, not that nobody moved
reproduction.actual: backend: historyDepthDays 0, window 0, asOf null.  page: 'RISERS — SELL-HIGH CANDIDATES / No qualifying movers in this window. / FALLERS — BUY-LOW CANDIDATES / No qualifying movers in this window.' under 'Rank deltas vs. 14d ago'

numericProof.formula: a rank delta over W days requires historyDepthDays >= W; here historyDepthDays = 0 so no window is computable, yet the UI asserts a 14/30-day comparison was made

findings.userImpact: The user reads the most prominent movement widget on the landing page, sees both the sell-high and buy-low columns empty under a heading claiming a 30-day comparison, and concludes the dynasty market has been flat. The truth is that the platform holds one snapshot and cannot answer the question at all. The correct user action — go look at movement elsewhere, or find out why history is missing — is never prompted.

priorFinding.note: PRIOR-A05-F04 found the same class of error on the SIGNALS engine ('HOLD is returned for "we have no history at all" with the reason "Stable — no movement"'). This reproduces it on a different surface (MoversPanel + MarketTicker) with different code, so the class is systemic rather than local. Separately I REFUTE PRIOR-A05-F12 ('MoversPanel labels risers as buy-low and fallers as sell-high — both inverted') at HEAD e96c06ef: MoversPanel.jsx:196-199 now reads 'Risers — sell-high candidates' / 'Fallers — buy-low candidates', with an in-code note citing that finding. It is fixed.

findings.whatWorks: The BACKEND is exemplary here and is not at fault: it separates measured window from requested window, publishes historyDepthDays and a null asOf, and its docstring explains why. Everything the frontend needs to tell the truth is already in the payload. MoversPanel's loading skeleton is also correctly sized to the settled shape (a documented fix for a ~500px layout jump).
findings.rootCause: MoversPanel treats an empty result array as the only state worth distinguishing, and hardcodes its subtitle from the user's window selection rather than from the response's `window`.
findings.requiredRepair: Branch on `historyDepthDays === 0 || asOf === null` first and render 'No rank history yet — we hold a single snapshot, so no movement can be measured', suppressing the subtitle's delta claim. When `window < windowRequested`, say so ('measured over N days, not 30'). Apply the same guard to MarketTicker.jsx:126. This is a display fix only — no backend change is needed.

verification.reasoning:
The observation reproduces verbatim on the correct topology (request interception, not plain :3000). MoversPanel.jsx:154-164 reads only `data.risers` / `data.fallers` and builds its subtitle from local `windowDays` state; `window`, `windowRequested` and `historyDepthDays` are never referenced anywhere in the file. The backend docstring at server.py:3385-3391 explicitly created `window` to stop exactly this mislabel ('reporting the request in that case labelled a 2-day delta "90 days"'). MoversPanel is rendered on `/` via frontend/app/page.jsx:17 -> TerminalLayout.jsx:76, so the page claim is right. Genuine, unfixed frontend defect. But four corrections force a rescope:

(1) The MarketTicker half is REFUTED. The finding says 'MarketTicker.jsx:126 compounds it'. It does not — MarketTicker never touches /api/movers or rank_history. frontend/lib/market-movers.js:1-22 states it reads the contract's per-row `rankChange` 'verbatim rather than recomputing from rank_history', and that field is populated on the live contract: 694 ints, 572 of them nonzero. The 'Market quiet in my roster' string I captured is produced because NO team was selected (the page simultaneously renders 'Pick your team' / 'Pick a team to see allocation'), i.e. an empty roster scope — a different defect with a different cause, not this one.

(2) The alarming state is container-conditional. `historyDepthDays: 0 / asOf: null` holds because `data/rank_history.jsonl` does not exist in this container (ls: No such file or directory) — the audit harness suppresses the scrape that writes it. In production the file exists; the backend docstring says it 'is only a few days deep today'. So the specific reading the userImpact turns on ('the user concludes the dynasty market has been flat') is not the production state. What IS live in production is the narrower and durable defect: whenever `window < windowRequested` — which the backend says is the normal case — the subtitle labels an N-day delta with the requested span. That is a mislabel, not a fabricated market fact.

(3) The title and userImpact both say the subtitle reads 'Rank deltas vs. 30d ago'. Default state is `useState(14)` (MoversPanel.jsx:127) and the rendered page says '14d ago'; the finding's own reproduction.actual also says 14d. The 30d wording only appears after a user clicks the 30d segment. Self-inconsistent.

(4) blastRadius playersAffected:1092 is unfounded — no player is mispriced; the panel shows at most 16 rows (limit=8 per side) and every delta it would show is a real one.

Display-layer mislabel with no wrong value acted upon => P2.
verification.whatWouldSettleIt: Seed data/rank_history.jsonl with 3 days of snapshots and request window=30. If the panel still prints 'Rank deltas vs. 30d ago' over a 3-day delta, the production-live half of this finding is proven independent of the harness. Conversely, confirming MarketTicker with a team selected and >=3 nonzero rankChange rows on that roster settles that its 'Market quiet' string is unrelated to rank history.

findings.title: The trade calculator publishes the fairness verdict "Near even" on an empty trade with zero assets on both sides
